answer.actor: The orphaned heirs of a man who willed a palm tree to his daughter
answer.event: The heirs divided the estate and gave the daughter no palm tree, and Rav Yosef first thought this was like the mishna's case.
answer.turn: Abaye objected that the cases differ, since here the tree is held by all the heirs.
answer.outcome: Abaye ruled the heirs must give her a palm tree and redivide the estate.
answer.summary: A man told his heirs to give his daughter a palm tree. The heirs split the estate and gave her none. Rav Yosef thought she had no claim, as in the mishna, but Abaye said the cases differ because the tree belongs to all of them. They had to give her a tree and divide the estate again.

answer.actor: A man who deposited silk with Rav Dimi
answer.event: The man left silk with Rav Dimi, who died without saying anything, and the claimant went to Rabbi Abba.
answer.turn: Rabbi Abba reasoned that Rav Dimi was not wealthy and that the claimant had described the silk.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded the silk to the claimant.
answer.summary: A man left silk at Rav Dimi's house, and Rav Dimi died without saying whose it was. The man came before Rabbi Abba. Rabbi Abba knew Rav Dimi was not rich and the man gave a distinguishing mark of the silk, so he ruled the silk was the man's.

answer.missing: This is a legal debate: Rav Hillel cites a written list against Ameimar's ruling and Rav Ashi answers. No event is narrated.

answer.actor: A man who recalled being immersed as a child to eat teruma
answer.event: He casually said he remembered being taken out of school and immersed so he could eat teruma, and that his friends called him Yohanan who eats hallot.
answer.turn: His offhand remark was taken as reliable evidence of priestly status.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi elevated him to the priesthood on his word.
answer.summary: A man mentioned in passing that, as a child, he was taken from school and immersed so he could eat teruma that evening. His friends kept away from him and called him Yohanan who eats hallot. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepted this as proof and declared him a priest.

answer.actor: Mar Ukva
answer.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records and saw he had given seven thousand gold dinars.
answer.turn: He felt this was too little for the journey to the World-to-Come.
answer.outcome: He got up and gave away half of his remaining money to charity.
answer.summary: As Mar Ukva was dying he asked for his charity records and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. He said his provisions were light and the road long. He then gave half of what he still owned to charity, and the Gemara explained why this did not break the one-fifth limit.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yohanan
answer.event: Rabbi Yohanan objected to Rabbi Elazar's claim that the uneducated will not be resurrected, and Rabbi Elazar answered with another verse.
answer.turn: Seeing Rabbi Yohanan grieved, Rabbi Elazar said he had found a remedy for the uneducated.
answer.outcome: He offered a way for them to share in life: supporting Torah scholars counts as cleaving to God.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar said the uneducated would not live again. Rabbi Yohanan objected that God would not like that said of ordinary Jews. When Rabbi Elazar saw him distressed, he offered a way out: those who marry their daughters to scholars or support scholars are credited as cleaving to God.
answer.missing: It is mostly a scriptural exchange with little event; the ending is a teaching rather than a narrated outcome.

answer.actor: Rav, as agent for Rabba bar bar Hana
answer.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy him a plot of land, and Rav bought it for himself.
answer.turn: This seemed deceitful, but the land was in a valley of violent men who respected Rav and not Rabba.
answer.outcome: The Gemara justified Rav, who feared someone else would buy the land before he could inform Rabba.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy land for him, but Rav bought it for himself. This looked like deceit. The Gemara explained that the local violent men would sell only to Rav, and that Rav acted at once because someone else might have bought it while he went to inform Rabba.

answer.actor: Rav Avya
answer.event: Rav Avya came to Neharde'a and saw a man tying a bolt to a door with a reed.
answer.outcome: He ruled that the door may not be locked on Shabbat with it.
answer.summary: Rav Avya visited Neharde'a and saw a man tying a bolt to his door with a reed. He said that the door could not be locked with it on Shabbat.
answer.missing: No turn or consequence is given; it is a brief ruling reported as an incident.

answer.actor: Rav Aha bar Abba and his son-in-law Rav Hisda
answer.event: Rav Aha visited Rav Hisda and sat his granddaughter on his lap.
answer.turn: Rav Hisda asked whether she might already be betrothed, and each accused the other of breaking a ruling of Rav or Shmuel.
answer.outcome: Rav Aha answered that Shmuel permits such acts done for the sake of Heaven.
answer.summary: Rav Aha visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and put his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether she might be betrothed. Rav Aha replied that Rav Hisda broke Rav's ruling by betrothing his daughter as a minor, and Rav Hisda answered that Rav Aha broke Shmuel's ruling about using a woman. Rav Aha said another view of Shmuel permits it when done for the sake of Heaven.

answer.actor: A Madonite man in Jerusalem
answer.event: He had a great deal of movable property he wanted to give as a gift and was told it must be transferred through land.
answer.turn: He bought a plot near Jerusalem and declared a part of it, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, to go to someone.
answer.outcome: He died, and the Sages upheld his statement.
answer.summary: A man in Jerusalem wanted to give away much movable property. The Sages told him he had to transfer it with land. He bought a plot and said a part of it, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, belonged to a named person. He died and the Sages carried out his words.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
answer.event: His sharecropper, who usually brought fruit on Friday, brought it on Thursday because he had a court case before him.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and disqualified himself as judge, then found himself thinking of ways the man could win.
answer.outcome: He had other scholars judge the case and cursed those who take bribes, since even he was biased without taking anything.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper brought a basket of fruit on a Thursday, not Friday, because he had a case to bring. Rabbi Yishmael refused it and said he could not judge the case. Two scholars judged it, but he kept thinking of ways the man might win, and concluded that those who really take bribes must be even more biased.

answer.actor: Rami bar Hama's sister and her husband Rav Avya
answer.event: Her marriage contract was lost and the couple came before Rav Yosef.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef cited Rabbi Meir's view that they were forbidden to each other, the Rabbis said it was permitted, and Abaye objected that the law follows Rabbi Meir's decrees.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef told Rav Avya to go and write her a new marriage contract.
answer.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya, and her marriage contract was lost. They asked Rav Yosef, who cited Rabbi Meir's strict view and the Rabbis' lenient one. Abaye said the law follows Rabbi Meir, so Rav Yosef told Rav Avya to write her a new contract.

answer.actor: A man testifying before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
answer.event: He said another man had the presumed status of a Levite because he had been called to read second in the synagogue.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua asked if this was due to his being a Levite or to prominence, and the man said a priest had read before him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accepted his word and elevated the man to Levite status.
answer.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was a Levite because he was called to read second in the synagogue. Rabbi Yehoshua asked if that was because he was a Levite or just prominent. The man said a priest read before him, and Rabbi Yehoshua accepted his word and elevated him to Levite status.

answer.actor: A man and Rabbi Yosei
answer.event: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether a widow could perform halitza within three months of her husband's death.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yosei said no, and when the man asked what harm there would be, Rabbi Yosei cited a verse.
answer.outcome: The verse shows that only someone eligible for levirate marriage may perform halitza.
answer.summary: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether halitza could be done within three months of the husband's death. Rabbi Yosei said it could not. When the man asked what harm it would do, Rabbi Yosei recited a verse from which he derived that anyone eligible for halitza must also be eligible for levirate marriage.
answer.missing: It is a question and answer with a legal conclusion rather than a story with events.

answer.actor: A man in Shihin whose father left him mustard stalks
answer.event: One of three mustard branches left by his father broke, and nine kav of mustard were found on it.
answer.outcome: They roofed a craftsmen's booth with its wood.
answer.summary: In Shihin a man's father left him three mustard branches. One broke and nine kav of mustard were found on it, and its wood was used to roof a potters' booth. Rabbi Shimon ben Tahlifa added that his father left a cabbage stalk they climbed with a ladder.
answer.missing: It is a marvel offered as proof of future abundance, with no real turn.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Yehuda bar Mareimar
answer.event: Rav Pappa went to arrange his son's marriage contract with Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came to honor him but would not enter the house.
answer.turn: Rav Pappa pressed him to enter, and his silent presence led Abba of Sura to write all his property into the dowry.
answer.outcome: Yehuda said that even this was not to his liking, so Abba of Sura offered to retract, and Yehuda said he should keep his agreement.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa went to write his son's marriage contract, and Yehuda bar Mareimar met him but hesitated at the door. Rav Pappa persuaded him to enter. He sat silent, and Abba of Sura thought he was angry and wrote all his property into the dowry. Yehuda said he did not like even that. Abba offered to retract, and Yehuda said he should not.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, Marei bar Mar and Rav Huna's son Rabba
answer.event: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent word asking Rav Huna whether the law follows Rabbi Elazar on bills of divorce.
answer.turn: Before the request arrived, Rav Huna died.
answer.outcome: His son Rabba answered from his father's tradition that the law follows Rabbi Elazar.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent a request to ask Rav Huna whether the law follows Rabbi Elazar on bills of divorce. Rav Huna died before it reached him. His son Rabba said that his father had taught, in Rava's name, that the law follows Rabbi Elazar, and others had the same ruling from Rav.

answer.actor: Orphan daughters and Rabbi Banai
answer.event: Orphan daughters came before Shmuel about movable property held for them by Rabbi Banai.
answer.outcome: Shmuel told Rabbi Banai to go and sustain them.
answer.summary: Rabbi Banai held movable property that belonged to orphans, and the orphan daughters came before Shmuel. He told Rabbi Banai to go and sustain them.
answer.missing: No turn or ending beyond the instruction; it is cited as a proof for a legal question.

answer.actor: A divorced woman, Shmuel and Rav Dimi bar Yosef
answer.event: A divorcee who did not want to nurse her son came before Shmuel, who sent Rav Dimi to check if the child recognized her.
answer.turn: Rav Dimi put her among women and carried the child past them, and the child looked at her joyfully while she looked away.
answer.outcome: Rav Dimi told her to lift her eyes and take her son.
answer.summary: A divorced woman came before Shmuel, unwilling to nurse her son. Shmuel sent Rav Dimi bar Yosef to see if the child knew her. Rav Dimi put her in a row of women and carried the child past, and the child looked at her gladly while she looked away. He told her to lift her eyes and take her son.

answer.actor: Ravina
answer.event: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphaned nephew and was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell.
answer.turn: He asked Rav Ashi whether he could bring the orphan's wine too.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi told him to go, since the orphan's wine was no better than his own.
answer.summary: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphaned nephew, and also had his own wine to take to Sikhra. He asked Rav Ashi if he could take the orphan's wine too. Rav Ashi said yes, because the orphan's wine was no better than his own.

answer.actor: A man who held a betrothal feast, and Rava
answer.event: A man prepared a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after a woman's first husband died, and Rava made him forfeit the feast.
answer.turn: The Gemara raises this as an objection, then answers that the feast was really a marriage feast.
answer.outcome: The objection is dismissed: a betrothal feast would have been allowed, but this one was a marriage feast.
answer.summary: A man once held a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after a woman's first husband died. Rava made him lose the feast. The Gemara explains that it was in fact a marriage feast, which was why Rava forbade it.
answer.missing: Who the man was and what happened to him after he lost the feast. The incident is only cited as an objection.

answer.actor: Rava Tosfa'a
answer.event: Rava Tosfa'a ruled a child fit when a woman's husband went overseas and her baby was delayed in the womb for twelve months.
answer.turn: The Gemara asks whose opinion he followed, since it is a minority view.
answer.outcome: The Gemara answers that he followed the majority, because Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also holds a baby can be delayed.
answer.summary: A woman's husband went overseas and she bore a child twelve months later. Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child fit and not a mamzer. The Gemara first asks how he could rely on the minority view of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, then explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel agrees, so he was following the majority.
answer.missing: The woman's identity and what happened to her or the child afterward. The incident is told only as a legal precedent.

answer.actor: A man claiming to be from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha
answer.event: A man said he was from Shot Mishot, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha stood up and said that the place lies between the rivers.
answer.turn: The Gemara asks why that matters and explains it bears on lineage status.
answer.outcome: The incident leads into a discussion of where the area between the rivers lies. The man's fate is not told.
answer.summary: A man told the Sages he came from Shot Mishot. Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha stood up and said the place lies between the Tigris and Euphrates. The Gemara then explains this matters for lineage, but never says what became of the man.
answer.missing: What happened to the man and whether his claim was accepted. The passage turns into a geography and lineage discussion.

answer.actor: Rav and Rav Yehuda
answer.event: Walking on the road behind a woman, Rav told Rav Yehuda to hurry away from Gehenna so they would not be secluded with her.
answer.turn: Rav Yehuda objected that Rav had permitted this for men of good morals.
answer.outcome: Rav explained that he meant only men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues, not ordinary men like themselves.
answer.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were walking on the road with a woman ahead of them. Rav urged Rav Yehuda to quicken his pace so they would avoid being secluded with her. Rav Yehuda pointed out that Rav himself allowed this for men of good morals. Rav answered that only exceptional men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi qualify, not the two of them.

answer.actor: A groom and his bride, and Rabban Gamliel the Elder
answer.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel he found no blood on his wedding night, and his bride said she was from the Dorketi family, who have no such blood.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel checked her relatives and found her claim was true.
answer.outcome: He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition and called him fortunate to have married into the Dorketi family.
answer.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel the Elder saying he found no blood on his wedding night. His bride said she was from the Dorketi family, whose women have no such blood. Rabban Gamliel questioned her relatives and found it true, then told the groom to keep his bride and called him fortunate.

answer.actor: A woman and the child she carried to Jerusalem
answer.event: A woman came to Jerusalem with a child on her shoulders, raised him, and he later had intercourse with her.
answer.turn: They were brought to court, where it was not certain he was her son.
answer.outcome: They were stoned because he clung to her, which gave him the presumptive status of her son.
answer.summary: A woman arrived in Jerusalem carrying a child on her shoulders, and she raised him. When he grew up he had intercourse with her. The court stoned both, not because he was definitely her son, but because he had clung to her like a son.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya and a heretic
answer.event: A heretic mocked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya as a man of thorns, citing a verse that calls the best of Israel a brier.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and pointed to the end of the verse.
answer.outcome: He gave two readings of the verse that turn the insult into praise.
answer.summary: A heretic insulted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya by quoting a verse that says the best of them is like a brier. Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and sent him to the end of the verse. He then explained that the thorns protect a breach, and that the righteous grind the nations down.
answer.missing: The heretic's reaction. The exchange ends with Rabbi Yehoshua's reply.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil, and Shmuel
answer.event: Rav Yosef acted in accordance with Rav's opinion, and Shmuel took offense and sarcastically remarked on the Sage's wisdom.
answer.turn: The Gemara uses Shmuel's anger to prove Rav and Shmuel really disagreed, then suggests Rav Yosef's case may have involved a daughter who denied her father's right.
answer.outcome: The Gemara concludes that Rav Yosef must have ruled in the case where she did not deny, which explains why Shmuel took exception.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef issued a ruling following Rav's view about a betrothal. Shmuel took offense and sarcastically asked whether wisdom is measured in a large measure only for this Sage. The Gemara uses that reaction as a legal argument about whether Rav and Shmuel truly disagreed.
answer.missing: The details of the case Rav Yosef decided and any outcome for the parties. The incident is used only as evidence in an argument.

answer.actor: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
answer.event: The two schools disagreed for two and a half years over whether it would have been better for man not to have been created.
answer.turn: They counted votes.
answer.outcome: They concluded it would have been better had man not been created, but now that he has been, he should examine his actions.
answer.summary: For two and a half years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argued over whether man should have been created. In the end they took a vote and decided it would have been better for man not to have been created. Since he has been, he should examine or scrutinize his deeds.
answer.missing: Who spoke or what particular events occurred. It is a summary of a long dispute and its resolution, not a told scene.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (Rabbi), on his deathbed
answer.event: Rabbi, near death, called in his sons and then the Sages of Israel and gave instructions for his household, his burial and his succession.
answer.turn: His wishes were later interpreted in light of events: he kept coming home on Shabbat eves until a neighbor knocked and he stopped, and the two attendants he named died before him.
answer.outcome: The instructions were followed: Gamliel became Nasi, he was eulogized in the cities, and the study sessions were to resume after thirty days.
answer.summary: On his deathbed Rabbi told his sons to honor their stepmother and to keep his lamp, table and bed in place, and he named two attendants to serve him in death. Each Shabbat eve he kept coming home, until a neighbor knocked and his maidservant said he was sitting inside, after which he never came again. He then told the Sages not to eulogize him in the small towns, to resume study after thirty days, and that Gamliel should be Nasi and Hanina bar Hama should head the yeshiva. The attendants died before him, and the people understood the instructions in the light of events.

answer.actor: Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: Rabbi Akiva collected an etrog on the first of Shevat and separated two tithes from it, one by Beit Shammai's view and one by Beit Hillel's.
answer.turn: Rav Mesharshiyya cites it as proof that Beit Shammai acted on their own opinion.
answer.outcome: The outcome is not in the passage.
answer.summary: Rabbi Akiva once picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and tithed it twice, as though it belonged to two different tithing years. This is cited as an objection to the claim that Beit Shammai did not act on their own view.
answer.missing: The rest of the incident and its resolution. It is cited only as a legal objection.

answer.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents, the deceased's heirs, and Rav Nachman
answer.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents deposited with a woman, who said she had seized it from the deceased while he was alive.
answer.turn: Rav Nachman asked for witnesses that the deceased had claimed it from her while alive, and she had none.
answer.outcome: He ruled her seizure counted as seizing after death, which is worth nothing.
answer.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and the dead man's heirs came to claim it. She said she had seized it from him while he was alive, to recover a debt. Rav Nachman asked for witnesses, and she had none, so he ruled it was seizure after death and invalid.

answer.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of the son of Elyashiv, the orphans, and Ravina
answer.event: She claimed her marriage contract from the orphans, who found it embarrassing that she appeared in house clothes.
answer.turn: She went and dressed in all her clothes, and the case came before Ravina.
answer.outcome: Ravina ruled, following Rav, that a widow's clothes are appraised and counted in the payment.
answer.summary: A widow was taking the orphans to court to collect her marriage contract. They told her it was demeaning for her to appear in house clothes. She dressed in all her finery, and when they came before Ravina he ruled that the court values what a widow is wearing and counts it against her payment.

answer.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar
answer.event: A case about a man's priestly status came before Rabbi Yochanan, with Reish Lakish and Rabbi Elazar sitting there, and Reish Lakish asked whether the man had received a share at the threshing floor.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yochanan answered with the same line Rabbi Elazar had used earlier, that the priesthood does not cease where there is no threshing floor.
answer.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not saying earlier that the ruling came from Rabbi Yochanan.
answer.summary: Earlier Reish Lakish challenged a man's priestly status and Rabbi Elazar replied with a rebuttal. Later, with all three sitting before Rabbi Yochanan, a similar case arose, and Reish Lakish raised the same question. Rabbi Yochanan gave Rabbi Elazar's same reply, so Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar for not saying it had come from Rabbi Yochanan.

answer.actor: The Sages, Rav and Shmuel
answer.event: The Sages suggested asking Mar Ukva's court in Kafrei, then reversed the names of the opinions and sent the question to Rav.
answer.turn: Rav swore that she needs both a bill of divorce and refusal and said Shmuel would never say otherwise.
answer.outcome: Rav's oath shows the opinion was wrongly attributed to Shmuel.
answer.summary: Shmuel's ruling on a minor betrothed without her father's consent was challenged, and the Sages swapped the names and sent the question to Rav. Rav swore that she needs both a divorce and refusal, and that Shmuel would never say otherwise.
answer.missing: Who the Sages speaking were, who asked, and what happened after Rav's answer.

answer.actor: Bunyam ben Nunyam and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: Bunyam ben Nunyam sent Rabbi a gift of fine linens.
answer.turn: The Gemara notes the linens folded to the size of a nut.
answer.outcome: The gift is described, but no response or consequence follows.
answer.summary: A wealthy man named Bunyam ben Nunyam once sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a gift of four kinds of fine linen. They were so thin that they folded down to the size of a nut or pistachio and unfolded large enough to cover Rabbi's body.
answer.missing: Any reaction from Rabbi and the circumstances of the gift. The passage serves to explain a word.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and Abaye
answer.event: A man came before Rav Yosef about a daughter's support, and Rav Yosef told the heirs to give her dates from the mats.
answer.turn: Abaye objected that not even a creditor could collect from movable property.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef explained he meant dates still attached and ripe for plucking, which are not movable property.
answer.summary: Someone brought a case about a daughter's support to Rav Yosef, who ruled she should be given dates lying on mats. Abaye objected that even a creditor could not collect that way. Rav Yosef replied that he meant ripe dates still on the tree.
answer.missing: Who the person was and what finally happened to the daughter.

answer.actor: Rabbi Meir, and a man who fell into the Great Cistern
answer.event: Rabbi Meir cited an incident of a man who fell into the Great Cistern and emerged after three days.
answer.turn: The Sages told Rabbi Meir that one does not cite miraculous events.
answer.outcome: The rest is a debate over what made it miraculous.
answer.summary: Rabbi Meir cited an incident of a man who fell into the Great Cistern and survived three days. The Sages objected that miraculous events are not used for general rulings. The Gemara then debates what exactly would have been miraculous.
answer.missing: The details of the man's fall and rescue, which the passage only alludes to.

answer.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
answer.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether Rabba would get angry.
answer.turn: The Gemara asks whether the test might have made Rabba sin, then explains Rav Huna had forgone his honor.
answer.outcome: The incident is accepted as legitimate, with the tear made at the seam and at a moment when Rabba was already angry.
answer.summary: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether he would become angry. The Gemara asks whether this would make his son sin, and answers that Rav Huna had forgone his honor. It adds that he tore at the seam, and did so when Rabba was already angry for another reason.

answer.actor: Rabbi Helbo
answer.event: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question about who reads from the Torah after the priest and the Levite, and he had no answer ready.
answer.turn: Unable to answer, he went and asked Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha gave him a ranked list of who reads next.
answer.summary: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question about who reads from the Torah after the priest and the Levite. He did not have the answer to hand, so he went to Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, who told him the order of readers: appointed scholars, fit scholars, sons of leaders, synagogue heads, then anyone.
answer.missing: The passage itself ends mid-sentence; the answer sits in the following segment. It is a thin inquiry-and-answer exchange rather than a full story.
It is a bare citation of advice Elijah gave Rabbi Natan, with no event.

answer.actor: A man who rented out a millstone, and his renter
answer.event: A man rented out a millstone in exchange for grinding, then grew rich, bought another millstone and a donkey, and demanded rent in money.
answer.turn: The renter refused to pay money, saying he would only grind as agreed.
answer.outcome: The standoff stands at the renter's refusal; how it is resolved is only discussed later.
answer.summary: A man rented his millstone to another, who paid for it by grinding for him. The owner later became rich and bought a new millstone and a donkey. He told the renter he no longer needed the grinding and wanted money instead, but the renter answered that he would grind as agreed and would not pay cash.
answer.missing: The resolution (whether the renter must pay) is only found in the later discussion of Ravina, Rav Avira and the Sodom-conduct ruling.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was ill, Rabbi Hiyya visited him and found him crying.
answer.turn: Rabbi Hiyya asked why he cried, citing a teaching that dying in tears is a bad sign.
answer.outcome: Rabbi said he was crying for the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to fulfill.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill and Rabbi Hiyya came to visit, finding him in tears. Hiyya asked why he was weeping, since a teaching says dying while crying is a bad sign. Rabbi answered that he was crying over the Torah and the commandments he would no longer be able to perform.

answer.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
answer.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land for him, and Rav bought it for himself.
answer.turn: This seems deceitful, and Rav should have told him, but the land was among violent men who honored Rav and not Rabba bar bar Hana.
answer.outcome: Rav's act stands: he feared someone else would buy the land in the meantime.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy him a field, but Rav bought it for himself. The Gemara objects that this is deceitful and that Rav should at least have informed him. It explains that the field lay among violent men who respected Rav but not Rabba bar bar Hana, and that Rav feared someone else would buy it while he was reporting back.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a minor girl, and Ravina
answer.event: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace.
answer.turn: Ravina ruled that even if a father's consent is presumed, it is not presumed for a degrading betrothal.
answer.outcome: No concern that the father agreed, so the betrothal is not valid.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace, without her father's consent. Ravina ruled that the presumption that a father may have desired the match applies only to a dignified betrothal, not a degrading one like this.
answer.missing: It is a case followed by a ruling; there is no real action beyond the betrothal itself.

answer.actor: A man in Mata Mehasya and his brother
answer.event: A man had a yevama fall to him for levirate marriage, and his brother wanted to disqualify her with a bill of divorce, apparently for the inheritance.
answer.turn: The man offered to share the property, but the brother feared being cheated as in the Pumbedita story.
answer.outcome: The man offered that the brother could divide the property from now.
answer.summary: A man in Mata Mehasya had a yevama fall to him, and his brother wanted to disqualify her by giving her a divorce document. The man asked whether this was about the inheritance and offered to split it. The brother feared he would be cheated as the Pumbedita swindler did, so the man told him to divide the property right away if he liked.

answer.missing: It is a legal question put to an elder with no answer or event shown.

answer.actor: Rav Yehuda
answer.event: A husband took a bundle of branches from his wife's property and fed them to his animals, and Rav Yehuda ruled on it.
answer.turn: Rav Yehuda treated this as legitimate consumption of her property.
answer.outcome: Rav Yehuda's ruling stands, explained by his general view on consuming forbidden produce.
answer.summary: The judges of Pumbedita reported that Rav Yehuda acted in a case where a husband took branches from his wife's land and fed them to his animals. He treated it as consumption of her property, consistent with his rule that even eating forbidden produce counts as taking possession.
answer.missing: The case is only sketched, and it is mostly a report of a ruling with its reasoning.

answer.actor: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya and Rav
answer.event: Rav Hinnana taught a mishna to Hiyya bar Rav in Rav's presence with a stringent wording.
answer.turn: Rav rebuked him for abandoning the Rabbis and following Rabbi Meir.
answer.outcome: The Gemara explains Rav Hinnana's reasoning and that the first clause follows the Rabbis, the last clause Rabbi Meir.
answer.summary: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya was teaching a mishna to Hiyya bar Rav in front of Rav, but wording it in the stringent way. Rav asked whether he had abandoned the Rabbis to follow Rabbi Meir. The Gemara explains he had inferred the first clause from the last, which was wrong because only the last follows Rabbi Meir.
answer.missing: It is mainly a correction of a teaching error, with the aftermath not shown.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
answer.event: He sat studying Torah in the lower marketplace of Tzippori while his cloak lay in the upper marketplace.
answer.turn: One time someone came to take the cloak.
answer.outcome: He found a serpent on it.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was so absorbed in Torah that he sat studying in the lower marketplace of Tzippori while his cloak lay in the upper one. One time a man came to take the cloak and found a serpent lying on it.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman and the judges of Nehardea and Pumbedita
answer.event: Judges in Nehardea ruled that daughters be supported from movable property, and Rav Hana bar Bizna did likewise in Pumbedita.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman ordered them to reverse their rulings and threatened to take their houses.
answer.outcome: Not stated whether they reversed.
answer.summary: Cases came before the courts of Nehardea and Pumbedita, and the judges ruled that daughters be supported from their father's movable property. Rav Nahman told them to reverse their decisions or he would collect the money from their own houses.
answer.missing: How the judges responded is not stated.

answer.actor: The tumtum of Biri
answer.event: A tumtum in Biri was placed in a seat and operated on, his skin was torn open, and he later fathered seven children.
answer.turn: Rabbi Ami used this as a challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's view that a torn tumtum is impotent.
answer.outcome: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda would doubt the children were his.
answer.summary: Rabbi Ami recalled a tumtum from Biri who was seated, torn open, and then fathered seven children, which seems to contradict Rabbi Yehuda's ruling. The Gemara replies that Rabbi Yehuda would say to go and check where those children came from.
answer.missing: The incident is a brief reference used as an argument, not told as a story.

answer.actor: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav
answer.event: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba saw Rav say kiddush before Shabbat began and asked whether he had now separated from labor.
answer.turn: Rav answered yes.
answer.outcome: This is cited as proof that reciting kiddush accepts the day's restrictions.
answer.summary: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba watched Rav recite kiddush before Shabbat began and asked whether he had thereby separated himself from work. Rav replied that he had.
answer.missing: It is a two-line exchange cited as proof for a law, not a developed story.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha
answer.event: A man brought him the first shearing, and in conversation said he also had a case to bring before him.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and disqualified himself as judge.
answer.outcome: He seated two scholars to judge the case, and while pacing he found himself mentally arguing for the man, which made him denounce bribe-takers.
answer.summary: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, the first shearing of his flock. Learning that he had a lawsuit pending, Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and said he was disqualified from judging the case. He seated two scholars to hear it, but as he came and went he caught himself thinking of arguments for the man, and concluded that those who really accept bribes must be even more biased.

answer.actor: Heirs of a man who left a will, and Rav Idi bar Avin and Rav Yosef
answer.event: A man instructed his heirs to give his daughter a dowry or 400 dinars of wine, and prices then moved so that money was left over.
answer.turn: The question arose who gets the surplus.
answer.outcome: Rav Idi bar Avin and Rav Yosef ruled the surplus goes to the male orphans.
answer.summary: A man told his heirs in his will to give his daughter a dowry, and the cost of dowries then fell. Another man told them to give her four hundred dinars of wine, and the wine's price rose, leaving a surplus. In each case the rabbis ruled that the leftover amount belongs to the male heirs.
answer.missing: The cases are brief hypothetical-style rulings; nothing about the people or what followed.

answer.actor: The orphans of a man who died in debt
answer.event: A man owing one hundred dinars died leaving land worth fifty, and the creditor repossessed it.
answer.turn: The orphans paid the creditor fifty dinars to get it back, but he repossessed it again to collect the rest.
answer.outcome: Abaye told them paying earlier was a mitzva, and now the creditor was repossessing lawfully.
answer.summary: A man who owed a creditor one hundred dinars died, leaving a small field worth fifty. The creditor seized it, the orphans paid him fifty to redeem it, and he seized it again for the remainder of the debt. They complained to Abaye, who told them that paying their father's debt was a mitzva, but the payment had not cancelled the lien, so the creditor was within his rights.

answer.actor: Abaye
answer.event: Abaye was riding along the bank of the Sagya River while Rav Mesharshiya and the rabbis sat on the other bank and did not stand for him.
answer.turn: Abaye protested that he was their primary teacher and they should stand.
answer.outcome: They answered that they had not noticed him at all.
answer.summary: Abaye was known to stand as soon as he saw the ear of Rav Yosef's donkey approaching. One day, riding along a river, he passed Rav Mesharshiya and other rabbis on the opposite bank who did not stand. He asked whether he was not their primary teacher, and they replied that it had never occurred to them, as they had not seen him.

answer.actor: A man picking dates and a woman who asked for some
answer.event: A woman asked a man picking dates to throw her two, and he asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he did.
answer.turn: She answered only 'Throw, throw,' which does not accept the condition.
answer.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled that such a statement is nothing and she is not betrothed.
answer.summary: A man was picking dates from a tree when a woman asked him to throw her two. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he did, and she just said 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled that this answer means nothing and she was not betrothed.

answer.missing: It is only a brief report that Rav Aha asked Rav Ashi's students whether he had said anything, and they said he had not; nothing happens.

answer.actor: A man's purchaser of a tract of land, facing a creditor
answer.event: A creditor repossessed one of two tracts a debtor had sold, then came to repossess the second, so the purchaser went to him with the whole debt in cash.
answer.turn: The purchaser offered the creditor a choice: take the tract as full payment or take the money and give up both tracts.
answer.outcome: Not shown; the creditor's response is not in the passage.
answer.summary: A man owed one hundred dinars and had sold two tracts of land for fifty each. The creditor repossessed one tract, then came for the other. The purchaser took one hundred dinars to the creditor and told him to either value the first tract at the full debt or take the money and give up both.
answer.missing: The creditor's answer and how the matter ended.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Shumni and Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya
answer.event: Two scholars parting at a river ford agreed each would tell the other a teaching he had not heard, and each opened with one.
answer.turn: Their exchange of teachings served as the example of the question asked.
answer.outcome: The second scholar's teaching and the exchange are cut off and do not clearly conclude.
answer.summary: Two scholars were saying goodbye at the ford of a river. They agreed each would offer a teaching the other had not heard. One defined the drinker as one who can still speak before a king. The other began a teaching about a convert's property, which Rav Sheshet and others then extended.
answer.missing: A real turn or ending; it is mostly a series of teachings.

answer.actor: A man pining for a woman, in Eretz Yisrael
answer.event: A man suffering over a certain woman wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael, but heard the teaching about the great significance of living there.
answer.turn: On hearing it, he gave up leaving.
answer.outcome: He endured his suffering in the land until the day he died.
answer.summary: A man in Eretz Yisrael was tormented by his love for a woman and wanted to leave the land to be with her. When he heard the idea about how significant it is to live in Eretz Yisrael, he stayed and endured his suffering there until his death.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hanina
answer.event: Rabbi Hanina sent four dinars through his wife to a pauper he supported every Shabbat eve.
answer.turn: His wife overheard people in the house asking the man whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths, and reported he did not need charity.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hanina responded that we should appreciate swindlers, since they spare us from sinning daily by neglecting the truly poor.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent a pauper four dinars. One day his wife took it and came back saying the man did not need it, because she heard people at his house asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina answered that we should be grateful to swindlers, because without them we would sin every day by not giving to the truly poor.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hanina Kara
answer.event: Sitting before Rabbi Yannai, Rabbi Hanina Kara said the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yannai disagreed with him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yannai told him to go outside and recite his verses there, since the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hanina Kara, an expert in Bible, sat before Rabbi Yannai and declared the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yannai told him to go outside and recite his verses there, because the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

answer.actor: Rabbi Meir
answer.event: Rabbi Meir, who used to ridicule transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman across a river and crossed a rope bridge toward her.
answer.turn: Halfway across, Satan left him and revealed the disguise.
answer.outcome: Satan said that only the heavenly proclamation protecting Rabbi Meir and his Torah kept him from destroying him.
answer.summary: Rabbi Meir used to mock people who sinned. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman on the far side of a river, and he took a rope bridge to reach her. At the midpoint Satan left him and said that if heaven had not proclaimed to take care of Rabbi Meir and his Torah, his blood would have been made worthless.

answer.actor: Rav Anan
answer.event: Rav Anan wrote a familiar letter to Rav Huna, who sent back a sharp reply through Rav Sheshet.
answer.turn: Rav Anan, offended and not understanding the word marzeiha, consulted Mar Ukva.
answer.outcome: Mar Ukva said Anan had taken an improper liberty in addressing Rav Huna and explained that marzeiha means a mourner.
answer.summary: Rav Anan sent Rav Huna a letter addressing him as an equal. Rav Huna replied sharply through Rav Sheshet, who relayed it reluctantly. Rav Anan, hurt and puzzled by the word marzeiha, went to Mar Ukva, who told him he had been presumptuous and explained the word means a mourner.

answer.actor: Rava
answer.event: In Rava's court a woman was obligated to swear, but his wife said she was untrustworthy, and he turned the oath onto the other party. On another occasion Rav Pappa said a document was already paid.
answer.turn: Rava would not accept one witness, Rav Pappa, yet had relied on his wife's word because he knew her to be reliable.
answer.outcome: Rava explained he knew his wife's honesty with certainty but not Rav Pappa's.
answer.summary: A woman had to swear an oath in Rava's court. Rava's wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, said the woman was known to swear falsely, so Rava shifted the oath to the other side. Later Rav Pappa said a document was already paid, but Rava said one witness is nothing. Rav Adda bar Mattana asked why Rava trusted his wife and not Rav Pappa, and Rava said he knew her honesty for certain, not Pappa's.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: Bonyos sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a measure of a se'a from Na'usa, and the Rabbi measured it.
answer.turn: It held 217 eggs, matching none of the standard se'a measures (the context shows this).
answer.outcome: The result is left unresolved in the passage.
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported that a man named Bonyos sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a se'a-measure from Na'usa. The Rabbi measured it and found it held 217 eggs, which fits none of the known se'a sizes.
answer.missing: What the measurement meant or how it was resolved.

answer.actor: A man who made a conditional bill of divorce
answer.event: A man told agents that if he did not return within thirty days, the document would be a divorce, and he arrived on the last day.
answer.turn: The ferryman was on the far side, so he could not cross in time and shouted to people that he had come.
answer.outcome: Shmuel ruled that this was not a return, so the condition was fulfilled.
answer.summary: A man set a condition that if he did not return within thirty days, his bill of divorce would take effect. He reached the river bank on the last day but the ferry was on the other side, so he shouted that he had come. Shmuel ruled that this does not count as returning.

answer.actor: Residents of Avel and Tzippori
answer.event: Rabbi Yehuda reported that people drew water on Shabbat from the channel running from Avel to Tzippori by the Elders' authority.
answer.turn: The Sages rejected it as proof, since the channel was too small to need a partition.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda's proof was dismissed.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda said that people used to draw water on Shabbat from a channel running from Avel to Tzippori with the Elders' permission and no extra partition. The other Sages replied that this was no proof, because the channel was too small to be a separate domain.
answer.missing: Little narrative detail; mainly a cited precedent and its rebuttal.

answer.actor: A Madonite man in Jerusalem
answer.event: A man with a lot of movable property wanted to give it away as a gift and was told he needed to transfer it by means of land.
answer.turn: He bought a plot near Jerusalem and designated part of it, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, for a named recipient.
answer.outcome: He died, and the Sages upheld his statement.
answer.summary: A man in Jerusalem wanted to give away a large amount of movable property but was told it could be transferred only along with land. He bought a plot near the city and declared part of it to a certain person together with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. He then died, and the Sages upheld what he said.

answer.actor: Neighbors of a gentile superintendent near Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya
answer.event: Neighbors asked a gentile superintendent to rent them his domain and he refused, so they asked whether they could rent it from his wife.
answer.turn: Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya and Rav Mattana had no answer.
answer.outcome: Rav Yehuda said in Shmuel's name that a man's wife may establish an eiruv without his knowledge.
answer.summary: A gentile superintendent who lived near Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya refused to rent his domain to the neighbors. They asked whether they could rent it from his wife, but neither Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya nor Rav Mattana knew. They went to Rav Yehuda, who said Shmuel ruled that a wife may establish an eiruv without her husband's knowledge.

answer.actor: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai
answer.event: Ben Azzai found a scroll of lineages in Jerusalem.
answer.turn: It recorded that someone was a mamzer, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teachings, and that Manasseh killed Isaiah.
answer.outcome: No further outcome in the passage.
answer.summary: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai said he found a scroll of lineages in Jerusalem. It listed a certain man as a mamzer, praised the teachings of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as accurate, and recorded that Manasseh killed Isaiah.
answer.missing: An actual unfolding story; the passage only reports a discovery and its contents.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle mat worth less than a peruta.
answer.turn: When people objected, he said four dinars wrapped in it would serve; she took it and stayed silent.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled her silence after the money was given means nothing, so there was no proven betrothal.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman using a mat of myrtle branches worth less than a peruta. People objected, so he said she was betrothed with the four dinars in it. She took it and said nothing. Rava ruled that silence after money is given counts for nothing.

answer.actor: A purchaser of a mansion facing a creditor
answer.event: A creditor repossessed one of two mansions sold for five hundred each, then sought the other, and the purchaser brought the whole thousand to him.
answer.turn: The purchaser offered the creditor either to keep the first mansion for the whole debt or take the thousand and release both.
answer.outcome: Rami bar Hama and Rava then discussed it, but the creditor's response is not given.
answer.summary: A man owed one thousand dinars and sold two mansions for five hundred each. The creditor repossessed one, then went after the other. The purchaser took a thousand dinars to the creditor and told him to either accept the first mansion as full payment or take the money and give up both.
answer.missing: The creditor's actual response.

answer.actor: A groom and bride who came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: A groom reported finding no blood on his wedding night and the bride said she was still a virgin.
answer.turn: Rabbi saw their faces were blackened by famine, so he had them bathed, fed and watered before sending them back to the room.
answer.outcome: The groom then found blood, and Rabbi told him to go take possession of his acquisition, citing Lamentations 4:8.
answer.summary: During a drought, a groom told Rabbi he found no blood on his wedding night, and his bride insisted she was still a virgin. Rabbi saw that their faces were dark from hunger and had them bathed, fed and given drink, then sent back to the room. This time the groom found blood, and Rabbi told him to go and enjoy his acquisition, quoting a verse about skin shriveled like wood.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: Rabbi once ruled in accordance with Rabbi Elazar on a woman's menstrual status.
answer.turn: He then remembered that Rabbi Elazar's colleagues disagreed with him.
answer.outcome: He said Rabbi Elazar is worthy to be relied upon in exigent circumstances.
answer.summary: Once Rabbi ruled that the law follows Rabbi Elazar. Afterward he remembered that Rabbi Elazar's colleagues disagreed with him. He nonetheless said that Rabbi Elazar is worthy to rely on in times of need.
answer.missing: The details of the case in which he ruled are not given.

answer.actor: A woman and Rava
answer.event: A woman who had seized a silver cup as partial payment of her marriage contract also demanded sustenance and came before Rava.
answer.turn: Rava ruled that part of the money does not count as all the money, so her seizure did not bar her claim.
answer.outcome: Rava told the orphans to go and give her sustenance.
answer.summary: A woman seized a silver cup toward her marriage contract and also demanded sustenance from her late husband's heirs. She came before Rava, who told the orphans to go and give her sustenance, since no one worries about Rabbi Shimon's view that partial money is not like all the money.

answer.actor: A man who came before Rabban Gamliel
answer.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel he had found an unobstructed orifice, and Gamliel answered with a parable about a man walking in the dark who finds a door open if he diverts it.
answer.turn: Gamliel suggested the man had diverted his approach, so the open finding proved nothing.
answer.outcome: No outcome for the man is stated; a second version only changes Gamliel's wording.
answer.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel claiming he had found an open orifice on his wedding night. Gamliel asked whether he had diverted his approach and told a parable of a man in the dark who finds a door open only if he diverts it. A second version has Gamliel say it was done intentionally. We are not told what became of the man.
answer.missing: What happened to the man and his claim afterward.

answer.actor: A woman who visited her husband's grave
answer.event: The text alludes to an incident in which a woman removed her husband from his grave.
answer.turn: Only a gesture at the incident appears in the Hebrew; the translation adds that she had intercourse with a guard and then suggested disinterring her husband to cover for a missing body.
answer.outcome: Used to show that even in mourning one may sin.
answer.summary: The Rabbis' view is illustrated by an incident of a woman who removed her husband from his grave. According to the translation's explanation, she met a man guarding a body of an executed person, they had intercourse, and when that body was taken she proposed digging up her husband so the guard could claim he had done his job. It is told only in allusion.
answer.missing: The Hebrew only alludes to the incident; the details come from the translator's gloss.

answer.actor: The son of a widow
answer.event: He asked Rabbi Eliezer whose request for water to honor first when both parents ask, and then took the same question to Rabbi Yehoshua.
answer.turn: He pressed Rabbi Yehoshua about a divorced mother.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua sarcastically told him he was obviously a widow's son and to pour water for them and squawk at them like chickens.
answer.summary: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer which parent to serve first if both ask for water. Eliezer said to set aside his mother's honor for his father's. He asked Rabbi Yehoshua, who said the same, and when the man asked what if his mother was divorced, Yehoshua remarked that his tear-filled eyelashes showed he was a widow's son and sarcastically told him to serve both.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and his student Abaye
answer.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain teaching, and Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it.
answer.turn: Abaye recalled the context in which Rav Yosef had stated it, including the brothers case and Rav Yehuda's explanation.
answer.outcome: No outcome is stated; the remembered teaching is simply laid out.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef claimed he had not heard a certain teaching. His student Abaye reminded him that he had said it to them, and recalled the brothers-at-father's-table case and the explanation Rav Yosef gave. The passage ends with the reminder, not Rav Yosef's reaction.
answer.missing: Rav Yosef's reaction to being reminded.

answer.actor: Rava
answer.event: Rava first thought famine was not like war regarding a wife's testimony of her husband's death, but a woman came before him and said her husband died in a famine.
answer.turn: Rava questioned her and she admitted he could not have survived the little flour she left, showing she had not seen him die.
answer.outcome: Rava retracted and said famine is like war.
answer.summary: Rava thought a wife's report of death in a famine should be trusted, unlike in war. Then a woman told him her husband had died in a famine. He asked whether she had done well to flee and leave him with a little flour, and she answered that he could not have survived that. Rava saw she had only inferred the death and changed his ruling to treat famine like war.

answer.missing: The passage is a legal argument with a passing example of Rabbi Tavla seeing a bolt and saying nothing, used as a proof and then rejected.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar
answer.event: As he went up to Eretz Yisrael, he said he had been spared one curse, then, when ordained, two, and when seated on the calendar council, three.
answer.turn: Each milestone avoided a part of the prophecy of Ezekiel that threatened those who would not be in the council, register or land of Israel.
answer.outcome: He was spared all three curses.
answer.summary: When Rabbi Elazar ascended to Eretz Yisrael he said he was spared one curse. When he was ordained he said he was spared two, and when he was seated on the calendar council he said three. The three correspond to the verse in Ezekiel that threatens false prophets with exclusion from the council, the register and the land.

answer.actor: A father and mother marrying off their minor daughter
answer.event: The father wanted her to marry his relative and the mother wanted her to marry hers, and the father yielded under pressure.
answer.turn: During the festive meal for the mother's relative, the father's relative came up to the roof and betrothed her.
answer.outcome: The Gemara assumes the father did not desire this betrothal, given his word and the effort spent on the meal.
answer.summary: A couple disagreed about whom to marry their young daughter to, and the wife forced her husband to accept her relative. While they ate and drank at the betrothal feast, the husband's relative came to the roof and betrothed the girl. The Gemara reasons that the father did not want that betrothal, since he had given his word and prepared the meal.

answer.actor: Mar Yehuda
answer.event: Mar Yehuda visited Rav Huna bar Yehuda's house and saw people carrying among trees that were not planted in rows.
answer.turn: He asked whether Rav Huna did not follow Avimi's view.
answer.outcome: Rav Huna replied that he followed Rav Naḥman, who permits it.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda came to Rav Huna bar Yehuda's house and saw people carrying among trees that were not planted in rows. He asked whether Rav Huna did not accept Avimi's ruling. Rav Huna answered that he followed Rav Naḥman's view, which permits it.

answer.actor: Rav Kahana
answer.event: Rav Kahana held beer belonging to an orphan and delayed selling it until the Festival.
answer.turn: He reasoned that although it might sour a little, it would fetch cash then.
answer.outcome: No result is told; only his reasoning is given.
answer.summary: Rav Kahana was holding beer that belonged to an orphan, Rav Mesharshiyya bar Ḥilkai. He held off selling it until the Festival, saying that although it might sour, it would bring in cash. We are not told how it turned out.
answer.missing: How the sale turned out.
This is Rav Yosef's reply in a legal dispute citing a past ruling by Rav Yehuda, not a narrative in itself.

answer.actor: Rav Naḥman bar Rav Ḥisda and Rabba
answer.event: A bill of divorce dated by the governor of Bascar was sent by Rav Naḥman bar Rav Ḥisda to Rabba for a ruling.
answer.turn: Rabba answered that even Rabbi Meir concedes since the governor is of that kingdom.
answer.outcome: Rabba's reply validates the bill.
answer.summary: A bill of divorce had been dated by the name of the governor of Bascar. Rav Naḥman bar Rav Ḥisda sent the question to Rabba. Rabba replied that even Rabbi Meir would accept it, since the governor belongs to that kingdom.
answer.missing: The people involved and what happened to the couple are not given; it is a case with a ruling.

answer.actor: A dying man and Toviya
answer.event: A man told those present that his property should go to Toviya, then died.
answer.turn: Toviya came to claim it.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yoḥanan said Toviya has come, with no worry that another Toviya was meant.
answer.summary: A man said at his deathbed that his property was for Toviya, and he died. Toviya came to claim it. Rabbi Yoḥanan said that Toviya has come, so there is no need to worry that someone else was meant.

answer.actor: Rabbi Zakkai and Rabbi Yoḥanan
answer.event: Rabbi Zakkai taught a baraita before Rabbi Yoḥanan that the area between side posts and beneath a crossbeam is a karmelit.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yoḥanan disagreed with it.
answer.outcome: He told him to go out and teach it outside the study hall.
answer.summary: Rabbi Zakkai recited a baraita before Rabbi Yoḥanan, holding that the space between side posts and under a crossbeam is a karmelit. Rabbi Yoḥanan rejected it and told him to go teach it outside.

answer.missing: The passage only asks how the Israelites knew the Jabesh-gilead girls were virgins and gives a method; it narrates no event.

answer.actor: A man who sold his property intending to move to Eretz Yisrael
answer.event: He sold his property with the intention of ascending but ultimately did not go.
answer.turn: The question arose whether he could undo the sale.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi ruled that if he had wanted to, he could have gone, so the sale stands.
answer.summary: A man sold his property planning to go up to Eretz Yisrael but in the end never went. Rav Ashi said that if he had wanted he could have ascended, so the sale stands. A second version words this as a question, leaving room to cancel if something outside his control prevented him on the way.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, and Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter
answer.event: Rabbi Elazar saw Nakdimon's daughter gathering barley from between horses' hooves in Akko.
answer.turn: Her fall from great wealth to this poverty struck him.
answer.outcome: He recited a verse about her, reading 'kids' as 'bodies'.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar swore that he saw Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter picking barley out from between the hooves of horses in Akko. She had once been enormously wealthy. He applied the verse about following the flock to her, reading it as having to feed her own body from animals' leftovers.

answer.actor: Rabbi Ami and a man in his neighborhood
answer.event: Rabbi Ami, after an investigation, publicly declared a neighbor to be a mamzer.
answer.turn: The man went about weeping at the declaration.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami consoled him that by making him publicly known he had given him life, since a known mamzer and his descendants survive.
answer.summary: A man living near Rabbi Ami was investigated and declared a mamzer. He went about weeping. Rabbi Ami told him not to be upset, because by making his status known he had given him life.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, Nehunya the well digger and his daughter
answer.event: Nehunya's daughter fell into the Great Cistern and Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa announced hour by hour that she was safe and then that she had come up.
answer.turn: She said a ram led by an old man pulled her out; Rabbi Hanina explained he knew because God would not let the righteous man's own child come to harm from his public work.
answer.outcome: She was saved. The passage itself adds only that Nehunya's son nonetheless died of thirst, illustrating that God is exacting with the righteous.
answer.summary: The daughter of Nehunya the well digger fell into the Great Cistern. Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa reported hour by hour that she was at peace and then that she had come up. She said a ram led by an old man had pulled her out, and he explained he had been sure the righteous man's own child would not be harmed by his public work.
answer.missing: The proposed passage [4] is only a later comment (Rabbi Abba) that Nehunya's son died of thirst, citing verses; the narrative itself is in the context segments, and the son's death is only mentioned, not narrated.

answer.actor: An Amorite and an Israelite resident of Eretz Yisrael
answer.event: The Amorite asked how much fruit the Israelite could pick from a palm tree by the Jordan and was told sixty kor.
answer.turn: The Amorite taunted that Israel had ruined the land since his people picked 120 kor.
answer.outcome: The Israelite retorted that he had only been speaking of one side of the tree.
answer.summary: An Amorite asked a resident of Eretz Yisrael how much he could pick from a palm tree on the Jordan's bank. He said sixty kor, and the Amorite scoffed that they used to pick 120, so Israel had ruined the land. The resident answered that he had only counted one side of the tree.

answer.actor: Aher (Elisha ben Avuya)
answer.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the interpreter, who had been executed, being dragged along the street by a pig.
answer.turn: He cried out, 'Shall a mouth that produced pearls lap dirt?'
answer.outcome: He left the fold and sinned.
answer.summary: According to one account, Aher saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit the interpreter being dragged in the street by a pig. He asked how a mouth that produced pearls could lap up dirt. That sight led him to go out and sin.

answer.actor: The people of the Upper Galilee and a poor man of noble descent from Tzippori
answer.event: They bought him a litra of meat every day.
answer.summary: The people of the Upper Galilee bought a litra of meat every day for a poor man of good family from Tzippori. Later sages ask why this was remarkable and suggest it was expensive poultry, a litra's weight in coins, or an animal slaughtered daily just for him.
answer.missing: There is no turn or resolution, only a bare report of an act of charity followed by discussion of what made it remarkable.

answer.actor: Rava and a Sage questioning him
answer.event: In a good mood Rava boasted he was like ben Azzai ready to answer any question; a Sage asked how many apples make an eiruv and Rava replied that one does not make an eiruv with apples.
answer.turn: The Sage objected from a mishna that all foods combine for the eiruv measure, showing apples do count.
answer.outcome: Rava's boast was undercut: his dismissive answer was shown wrong by the mishna.
answer.summary: Rava, feeling sharp, declared he was like ben Azzai and could answer anything. A Sage asked how many apples are needed for an eiruv, and Rava asked whether one even makes an eiruv with apples. The Sage answered with a mishna showing that all foods, apples included, count toward the measure.
answer.missing: The explicit conclusion that Rava conceded is not stated; it comes through the follow-up discussion.

answer.actor: Rav Kahana
answer.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana, a seller of palm-leaf baskets.
answer.turn: He said he would go adorn himself, climbed to the roof and threw himself off; Elijah came and caught him.
answer.outcome: Elijah complained he had been made to travel four hundred parasangs, Kahana blamed poverty, and Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.
answer.summary: Rav Kahana sold palm-leaf baskets and a noblewoman tried to seduce him. He said he would go adorn himself, went up on the roof and fell, and Elijah caught him, complaining of the long journey. Kahana said poverty had put him in this position, so Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.

answer.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yohanan
answer.event: A man testified before Reish Lakish that another was a priest because he read first in synagogue; Reish Lakish demanded evidence of receiving teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar objected that the priesthood does not lapse where there is no threshing floor.
answer.turn: Later the same kind of case came before Rabbi Yohanan, who said exactly what Rabbi Elazar had said; Reish Lakish realized Elazar had been quoting Yohanan.
answer.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing the statement in Yohanan's name.
answer.summary: A man came before Reish Lakish claiming another was a priest because he read first in synagogue. Reish Lakish asked whether he had seen him receive teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar replied that the priesthood does not cease where there is no threshing floor. Later Rabbi Yohanan said the same thing in a similar case, and Reish Lakish glared at Elazar for not having said it in Yohanan's name.

answer.missing: Rav's statement about the sandal he would use for halitza is a halakhic remark with a passing reference to what he saw Rabbi Hiyya do; no event is told.

answer.actor: Rav Sheshet and a man passing his father-in-law's house
answer.event: Rav Sheshet had a man lashed for merely passing the entrance of his father-in-law's house.
answer.turn: The Gemara explains the man was suspected of misconduct with his mother-in-law.
answer.outcome: He was lashed.
answer.summary: A man who only passed by the entrance to his father-in-law's house was lashed by Rav Sheshet. It is explained that he was suspected with his mother-in-law, so even passing by lent credence to the rumor.
answer.missing: The incident is a brief precedent inside a legal question; no detail of what happened beyond the lashing.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yirmeya
answer.event: Rabbi Yirmeya went out to the villages, where he was asked whether an eiruv may be made with moist beans.
answer.turn: He had no answer.
answer.outcome: On returning to the study hall he was told Rabbi Yannai's ruling that one may, with a handful.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yirmeya visited some villages and was asked whether moist beans can be used for an eiruv. He did not know. Back in the study hall he was told that Rabbi Yannai permits it.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his son
answer.event: Rabbi arranged his son's marriage into Rabbi Hiyya's family but the bride died as the contract was being written, so they checked the families' ancestry; he then arranged a match with the family of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra.
answer.turn: The son, promised twelve years of study first, saw the bride and first shortened it to six years and then asked to marry first; he was ashamed before his father, who reassured him.
answer.outcome: He married and then studied twelve years; on return his wife was infertile and, after he prayed, she was healed.
answer.summary: Rabbi arranged his son's marriage into Rabbi Hiyya's family, but the bride died as the contract was being written, and they investigated the family lines. He then arranged another match, and the son, who had agreed to study twelve years first, saw the bride and asked to marry first, and was ashamed before his father. After his twelve years of study his wife was infertile until he prayed for her and she was healed.
answer.missing: What disqualification the ancestry check revealed is only hinted at.

answer.actor: A woman whose bill of divorce was closer to her, and her husband and brother-in-law
answer.event: In a precedent, a bill of divorce was closer to the woman than the man and was then lost.
answer.turn: After the husband died, the court did not rely on it.
answer.outcome: They required her to perform halitza.
answer.summary: Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi of a past case where a bill of divorce was closer to the woman and was lost. After her husband died, they still required her to perform halitza rather than rely on the divorce.
answer.missing: Who the people were and what happened are not described; it is a bare precedent cited for a legal point.
Rav Nachman's instruction to clear the earth is cited only as evidence for a legal position; nothing is narrated beyond that and the Gemara's reasoning.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon and his mother
answer.event: Rabbi Tarfon used to bend down so his mother could climb onto and step down from her bed using him, and he boasted of this in the study hall.
answer.turn: The Sages told him he had not reached even half of the honor due, asking whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea in front of him without his shaming her.
answer.outcome: His boast was met with a rebuke showing his honoring fell short; no reply is given.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tarfon would bend down so his mother could climb into and out of bed on him, and he praised himself for this in the study hall. The Sages told him he had not reached half the honor due, asking whether he would have stayed calm had she thrown his purse into the sea.

answer.actor: Ameimar and Mar Ukva
answer.event: A feather landed on Ameimar's head while he was judging, and a man removed it.
answer.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
answer.outcome: Ameimar said he was disqualified from judging the case; Mar Ukva did the same with a man who covered spittle in front of him.
answer.summary: While Ameimar sat in judgment a feather landed on his head and a man removed it, then said he had a case before him. Ameimar said he was disqualified from judging it because of the favor. Mar Ukva did likewise with a man who covered spittle before him.

answer.actor: The Sages examining a bill of divorce signed Anan bar Hiyya
answer.event: A bill of divorce was found in Sura by an Anan bar Hiyya of Neharde'a, and the Sages searched all the way to Neharde'a and found only one other man of that name, from Hagra.
answer.turn: Witnesses said that Anan bar Hiyya of Hagra was with them in Neharde'a on the day the get was written.
answer.outcome: Abaye and Rava then each argue whether the doubt about identity matters; no conclusion on the case itself is told.
answer.summary: A bill of divorce turned up in Sura signed by Anan bar Hiyya of Neharde'a. The Sages searched and found only one other man of that name, from Hagra, but witnesses said he was with them in Neharde'a that day. The rest is Abaye and Rava debating whether the doubt matters.
answer.missing: No outcome for the woman is narrated; segments [5] and [6] are legal reasoning.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: A reservoir in Yavne presumed to hold the required amount was measured and found deficient, and Rabbi Tarfon declared the immersions in it pure while Rabbi Akiva declared them impure.
answer.turn: They argued by analogies to a priest on the altar found to be disqualified, and Akiva made his case by distinguishing the types of disqualification.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Tarfon accepted Akiva's reasoning, saying that anyone who separates from him is separating from life.
answer.summary: A reservoir in Yavne was measured and found short of the required amount. Rabbi Tarfon held the earlier immersions pure and Rabbi Akiva impure, and they argued by comparing it to a priest found disqualified at the altar. Akiva explained the difference between disqualifications and Tarfon accepted, telling him that to part from him is to part from life.
answer.missing: It is mostly a legal debate, with the incident only as its starting point.
Rabba bar Avuh's offer to give his daughter to Rav Nachman if his body steams is cited only to test a legal view of the signs of a eunuch; no event or outcome is narrated.

A baraita about the origin of a permission for the Heker well: it states a rule with a note on the exiles encamping there and the prophets or custom permitting it, but there is no event, turn or ending.

answer.actor: Mar Zutra
answer.event: Mar Zutra visited the dying convert Rabbi Yehuda from India, who had no heirs, and told Rabbi Yehuda's slave to take his shoes home.
answer.turn: The shoe request was a way of claiming the slave, since a convert's ownerless property goes to whoever claims it first.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda died and Mar Zutra gained a slave.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda from India, a convert with no heirs, fell ill. Mar Zutra visited him, saw he was near death, and told his slave to remove Mar Zutra's shoes and carry them to his house. This acquired the slave for Mar Zutra before the master died. The Gemara says one departed to death and the other to life.

answer.actor: Ravin the Pious
answer.event: Sent to betroth a woman for his son, Ravin betrothed her to himself.
answer.turn: This looked like deceit by an agent, so the Gemara asks how a pious man could do it.
answer.outcome: The Gemara explains the family would not give her to the son and that Ravin feared someone else would betroth her while he reported back.
answer.summary: Ravin the Pious was sent to betroth a woman to his son, but he betrothed her to himself. This seems deceitful for an agent. The Gemara answers that her family refused to give her to the son. Ravin did not stop to tell his son because someone else might have betrothed her in the meantime.

answer.actor: A man who sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael
answer.event: He sold his property intending to ascend to Eretz Yisrael, went, but could not settle there.
answer.turn: On his return he tried to nullify the sale because he had not settled.
answer.outcome: Rava rules he can nullify it, or in another version that he cannot since he did ascend.
answer.summary: A man sold his property, stating he was going to Eretz Yisrael. He went but could not settle there, and he tried to cancel the sale. Rava ruled that whoever goes intends to settle, so the sale is void. Another version says he intended only to go, and he went, so it stands.

answer.actor: Rav Kahana
answer.event: Rav Kahana, a priest, took a cloth from a man redeeming his firstborn son and said he valued it at five sela.
answer.turn: The incident is cited as an example of a priest accepting an item at a stated value.
answer.outcome: The son is understood to be redeemed. The passage then adds Mar bar Rav Ashi buying a cloth for thirteen when it was worth ten.
answer.summary: Rav Kahana, a priest, took a cloth from the house of a man redeeming his firstborn son and said he saw it as worth five sela. The Gemara uses this as an example of a priest accepting an item at a stated value. A second brief case follows in which Mar bar Rav Ashi paid thirteen for a cloth worth ten because he needed one.
answer.missing: The passage cites these incidents as legal illustrations, and the redemption outcome is only implied.

answer.actor: Elisha ben Avuya (Aher)
answer.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator dragged along by a pig after the government executed him.
answer.turn: He asked whether a mouth that produced pearls should lap up dirt.
answer.outcome: He went out and sinned.
answer.summary: According to one account, Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the interpreter, who had been executed, being dragged away by something unclean. He asked how a mouth that produced pearls could end up licking dust. This led him to abandon the faith and sin.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi
answer.event: While studying, the two stood up when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed by.
