answer.turn: Rabbi Shimon told them they did not need to stand, since they were ordained scholars and he was only an associate, and the Torah does not stand for those who study it.
answer.outcome: He waved off their gesture of respect.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi were sitting and studying when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba walked by, and they stood for him. He told them they need not, because they were ordained and he was not, and because people studying Torah do not stand for others.

answer.actor: A brewer
answer.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from beer he was making for someone else, and the owner found him and told him to give her better sediment.
answer.turn: The brewer asked Rava whether the owner's remark meant he had relinquished his rights.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled the owner spoke only out of embarrassment, so the woman is not betrothed.
answer.summary: A brewer making date beer for someone betrothed a woman with its sediment. The owner found him and said to give her a better one. The brewer took the question to Rava. Rava ruled that this remark helps only for teruma, and here the owner spoke from embarrassment, so she is not betrothed.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel
answer.event: A heretic cited a verse to claim God had performed halitza on Israel, and Rabban Gamliel answered him.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel pointed to the exact wording, 'from them' and not 'to them'.
answer.outcome: He turned the argument around: Israel removed themselves from God, and that carries no weight.
answer.summary: A heretic told Rabban Gamliel that God had cast Israel off like a yavam doing halitza, citing Hoshea. Rabban Gamliel called him a fool and said the verse says 'from them,' meaning Israel abandoned God. Such an act by the yevama has no significance.

answer.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
answer.event: Heirs claimed a bag of documents deposited with her, and she said she had seized it from the deceased while he was alive.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman asked for witnesses, and she had none.
answer.outcome: He ruled it was seizure after death, which is nothing.
answer.summary: A woman held a bag of documents deposited with her. The deceased's heirs demanded it, and she said she had seized it during his life against a debt. At Rav Nahman's court she had no witnesses. He ruled that seizure after death is worthless.

answer.actor: Ravina and Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
answer.event: A man passed before them without covering his head, and Ravina called him rude.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yirmeya suggested he might be from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are common and people are less careful.
answer.outcome: Ravina's judgment is softened.
answer.summary: Ravina was sitting before Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti when a man walked past without covering his head. Ravina said he was rude. Rabbi Yirmeya said he might come from Mata Mehasya, where scholars are so common that people are not careful about such honor.

answer.actor: The heirs of a man who willed a palm tree to his daughter
answer.event: A man left a palm tree to his daughter and died owning only two half palm trees, which the heirs wanted to give her.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi questioned whether two halves count as a whole tree.
answer.outcome: Rav Mordekhai relayed Rava's view that people do call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs may give them.
answer.summary: A man said in his will that he was leaving a palm tree to his daughter. He died owning only two half palm trees, and the heirs wanted to give her those. Rav Ashi doubted that two halves count as a tree. Rav Mordekhai reported in Rava's name that people do call them a palm tree, so the heirs may give them.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: A case about an alleyway closed by the sea on one side and a garbage dump on the other came before him.
answer.turn: He gave neither a permission nor a prohibition.
answer.outcome: He ruled neither way, because the dump might be removed or the sea might leave sediment, yet the partitions did exist.
answer.summary: A case came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about an alley closed by the sea on one end and a garbage dump on the other. He declined to permit carrying there, fearing the dump might be removed or the sea might silt up. He also declined to forbid it, since the partitions did exist.
answer.missing: The incident is cited as legal precedent. Who brought the case and what the people did is not described.

answer.actor: A woman who came to Rabbi Yehuda's court
answer.event: She came to testify that her husband had died, and the people at court told her to mourn, tear her clothes and unbind her hair.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehuda required visible grief, so they coached her, though they held the lenient view themselves.
answer.outcome: She would appear as a mourner so Rabbi Yehuda would permit her to remarry.
answer.summary: A woman came to Rabbi Yehuda's court to say her husband had died. The people there told her to lament, tear her clothes and unbind her hair. They agreed with the Rabbis' lenient view but feared Rabbi Yehuda would refuse without signs of grief. The coaching was to get him to permit her to remarry.

answer.actor: Androlinai's wife
answer.event: A bill of divorce signed 'Androlinai of Neharde'a' was found, and his wife asked to remarry on its basis.
answer.turn: No one knew whether her husband or another man of the same name had issued it.
answer.outcome: The father of Shmuel asked Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, who replied that all of Neharde'a must be examined.
answer.summary: A bill of divorce was found in Neharde'a, signed by Androlinai. His wife asked to remarry on its strength. No one knew whether it was her husband's. Shmuel's father sent the question to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia in Eretz Yisrael, who answered that all of Neharde'a must be checked for another man of that name.

answer.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
answer.event: The Sages designated four hundred gold coins for her perfume account from her late husband's estate.
answer.turn: She answered with a blessing that they should pledge the same for their own daughters.
answer.outcome: The Sages answered 'Amen' after her.
answer.summary: When the Sages set aside four hundred gold coins from her late husband's estate for the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon's perfume account for one day, she blessed them. She said they should pledge this for their own daughters, and they answered amen.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil and Shmuel
answer.event: Rav Yosef ruled like Rav in a betrothal case, and Shmuel took offense.
answer.turn: Shmuel's offense is used as proof that Rav and Shmuel really disagree.
answer.outcome: The Gemara concludes the two did disagree.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef acted according to Rav in a case of a father's betrothal of his daughter, ignoring the father's betrothal. Shmuel sarcastically complained that wisdom had been given to Rav Yosef in a large measure. The Gemara argues that Shmuel's anger shows he and Rav truly disagreed.
answer.missing: What exactly Rav Yosef did, and Shmuel's actual words and reaction in the scene, are only referred to inside a legal argument.

answer.actor: The daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Guryon
answer.event: After her husband died, the Sages apportioned her two se'a of wine for pudding from his estate.
answer.turn: She blessed them that they might apportion this much for their own daughters.
answer.outcome: The Sages did not answer amen, as she was a widow awaiting a yavam and they did not want their daughters in her state.
answer.summary: Nakdimon ben Guryon's widowed daughter-in-law was given two se'a of wine weekly for pudding from his estate. She blessed the Sages that they should do the same for their daughters. One tradition says she was waiting for her yavam, so the Sages did not say amen.

answer.actor: Shmuel
answer.event: A man helped Shmuel off a narrow ferry, then said he had a case to bring to him.
answer.turn: Shmuel realized the favor created a bond.
answer.outcome: Shmuel disqualified himself from judging the man's case.
answer.summary: Shmuel was crossing a river on a narrow ferry when a man gave him a hand to get out. Shmuel asked what the man was doing there, and he said he had a case for him. Shmuel said he was disqualified because of the favor.

answer.actor: A man who rented out a millstone and the renter
answer.event: A man rented his millstone in return for grinding, then grew rich and bought another millstone and a donkey.
answer.turn: He no longer needed the grinding and demanded money for the rental.
answer.outcome: The renter refused to pay money; the dispute is left to later argument.
answer.summary: A man rented out a millstone for the price of grinding for him. He became rich, bought another millstone and a donkey, and no longer needed the service. He demanded money for the millstone, and the renter said he would grind as agreed but had not agreed to pay money.
answer.missing: The outcome of the dispute is not given in the passage.

answer.actor: Rami bar Hama, Mar Ukva, Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman
answer.event: Their mother gave her property to Rami in a morning deed and to Mar Ukva in an evening deed, and the brothers took their claims to different judges.
answer.turn: Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman each upheld a different brother's claim and challenged each other's reasons.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman claimed his ruling rested on the judges' discretion, and said Rav Sheshet was not a judge and had used a different theory.
answer.summary: A mother wrote one deed for Rami bar Hama in the morning and another for Mar Ukva in the evening. Rav Sheshet awarded the property to Rami, and Rav Nahman awarded it to Mar Ukva. Rav Sheshet argued that Rami's deed was earlier, but Rav Nahman said hours are not recorded on documents. Rav Nahman said his own ruling was by the judges' discretion, and that Rav Sheshet was not a judge.

answer.actor: A man who deposited sesame plants, and the friend who held them
answer.event: A depositor asked for his sesame plants back and the bailee claimed he had already taken them.
answer.turn: The owner pointed to the barrel of the stated amount at the bailee's house; the bailee said those were other plants.
answer.outcome: The dispute went before the Sages, where Rav Hisda would rely on the owner's description and Rava rejected that; no verdict is told.
answer.summary: A man deposited sesame plants with a friend. When he asked for them back, the friend said he had already taken them. The owner pointed to a barrel of a particular amount in the friend's house, but the friend said those were different plants. The case went to the Sages, but no ruling on the facts is reported.
answer.missing: The actual ruling or what became of the sesame; only the scholars' competing arguments follow.

answer.actor: Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law
answer.event: She seized a saddlebag full of coins for her sustenance.
answer.turn: The Sages found they had no power to take it from her.
answer.outcome: She kept the money.
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported an incident from Eretz Yisrael. Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law seized a saddlebag full of coins to cover her sustenance. The Sages had no power to remove it from her, so she kept it.

answer.actor: The sons of the house of bar Tzartzur, and Rav Amram
answer.event: The sons of two wives disputed an estate that had grown in value, and came before Rav Amram.
answer.turn: Rav Amram told one side to appease the other; they ignored him and he threatened excommunication, then sent them to Rav Naham.
answer.outcome: Rav Naham ruled that the heirs had acquired their rights when the father died, so they divide the estate equally.
answer.summary: The sons of two wives of bar Tzartzur came to Rav Amram over an estate that had appreciated. He told them to appease the other sons, but they ignored him, so he threatened to excommunicate them and sent them to Rav Nahman. Rav Nahman ruled that, as with a depreciated estate, the heirs acquired rights at the father's death, so they divide equally.

answer.actor: Ravin the Pious
answer.event: Sent to betroth a woman for his son, he betrothed her to himself.
answer.turn: This looked like deceit by an agent; the explanation is that her family would not give her to the son and he feared someone else would betroth her while he reported back.
answer.outcome: The betrothal stood and his conduct was justified.
answer.summary: Ravin the Pious went to betroth a woman for his son but betrothed her to himself. The Gemara objects that this is deceit, then explains that her family would not give her to the son. Ravin did not go back to tell his son because someone else might have betrothed her meanwhile.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and Rav Beivai
answer.event: Rav Beivai told the Sages not to trust Rav Yosef's report of a teaching.
answer.turn: Rav Beivai said he had taught it in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava with a different reasoning; Rav Yosef realized he had confused rabbim with Rabbi.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef admitted his mistake.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef had reported a teaching in the name of Rabbi. Rav Beivai told the Sages not to listen, saying he had taught it to Rav Yosef in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava, and the word was rabbim, many. Rav Yosef exclaimed in astonishment that he had mistaken one word for the other.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and his student Abaye
answer.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard Shmuel's teaching on roofs, and Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef remembered, but corrected how the teaching had been transmitted.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef restated the teaching, and when Abaye pressed on the word residents, clarified that too.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef, whose memory had been affected by illness, said he had not heard Shmuel's teaching about roofs. Abaye reminded him that he had taught it and had even added a qualification. Rav Yosef then recalled it, but with a different wording of the qualification, and answered Abaye's objection by explaining how his word residents should be read.

answer.actor: Ravina and Rav Ashi's daughter
answer.event: Ravina arranged for Rav Ashi's daughter to collect one-tenth of an estate, from one heir as intermediate land without an oath and from an orphan as inferior land with an oath.
answer.outcome: The differing treatment is taken as proof she was a creditor of the sons.
answer.summary: Ravina had Rav Ashi's daughter collect her one-tenth of an estate from two heirs. From Mar she collected intermediate-quality land without an oath, and from an orphan son of Rav Sama she collected inferior land with an oath. This is used as proof of whose creditor she is.
answer.missing: Why the heirs stood where they did, and any conflict or turn; it is reported as a precedent.

answer.actor: A man who sold land, and Rav Pappa
answer.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa to buy oxen, then did not need the money.
answer.turn: He regretted the sale and asked for it back.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land, though beyond the letter of the law.
answer.summary: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed money to buy oxen. In the end he did not need the money and regretted the sale, and Rav Pappa gave the land back. The Gemara notes that Rav Pappa acted beyond what the law required.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
answer.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba found Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying his grandchild to the synagogue with a cloth thrown over his head.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua explained that a verse links teaching children to the day at Sinai.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hiyya and Rabba bar Rav Huna each adopted the practice of teaching a child before eating.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba met Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing a child to the synagogue with a covering hastily on his head and asked what the fuss was about. Rabbi Yehoshua answered that the verse about making things known to your sons is joined to the day at Sinai. From then on Rabbi Hiyya would not eat until he had taught a child, and Rabba bar Rav Huna would not eat until he had brought a child to the study hall.

answer.actor: Rabbi Zeira
answer.event: Rabbi Zeira, finding no ferry, crossed the Jordan holding a rope when going up to Eretz Yisrael.
answer.turn: A Sadducee mocked him as hasty.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Zeira answered that Moses and Aaron did not merit entering, so he hurried before anything could prevent him.
answer.summary: Rabbi Zeira went up to Eretz Yisrael and, with no ferry, crossed the Jordan by holding a rope. A Sadducee mocked him as the hasty people who said do before hear. Rabbi Zeira replied that even Moses and Aaron did not merit entering, so he did not know he would, and he hurried.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai
answer.event: He left for the study hall without waiting for Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai and stayed twelve years.
answer.turn: On return he did not recognize his town and was led home by hearing his daughter called; his wife saw him and died of shock.
answer.outcome: He pleaded for mercy and she was revived.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai would not wait for Rabbi Shimon's wedding feast to end and went to study for twelve years. He came back to a town whose paths had changed and sat by the river, where he heard a girl called Hakhinai's daughter and followed her home. His wife looked up, saw him, and died from the shock. He prayed for her and she came back to life.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Yehuda bar Mareimar
answer.event: Rav Pappa went to write his son's bride's marriage contract and Yehuda bar Mareimar came to greet him but would not enter the house.
answer.turn: Rav Pappa pressed him in; Yehuda bar Mareimar sat silent, and the bride's father took his silence for anger.
answer.outcome: The bride's father wrote over everything he owned as her dowry and told him he had left nothing for himself.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa went to have his son's marriage contract written, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came to greet him but would not go in. Rav Pappa eventually got him to enter, where he sat silent. The bride's father, Abba of Sura, took the silence for anger and wrote all he had as the dowry, saying at last that he had left himself nothing.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
answer.event: The Elders gathered in a loft in Lod and were asked whether study or action is greater.
answer.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action and Rabbi Akiva said study.
answer.outcome: All concluded that study is greater because it leads to action.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were reclining in a loft in Lod when they were asked whether study or action is greater. Rabbi Tarfon said action, Rabbi Akiva said study, and in the end everyone agreed study is greater since it leads to action.
answer.missing: Anything beyond a debate that ends in agreement; it is a scene with a verdict rather than an event with a turn.

answer.actor: A steward for a dead man's orphans, before Abaye
answer.event: A man had set up a field as a marker for another, later contested it, and died; his steward came before Abaye.
answer.turn: Abaye said the man had lost his right; the steward argued what the father would have claimed, one furrow and then repurchase.
answer.outcome: Abaye accepted the claims, gave the other side one furrow, and let the steward keep the palm-tree furrow, praising his skill.
answer.summary: A man had listed a field as a marker for someone else, then contested it and died. His steward came before Abaye, who first said the man had lost his right. The steward argued what the father could have claimed, a single furrow and later repurchase, and Abaye accepted both. The steward kept the furrow with the palm trees, and Abaye praised appointing a steward like him.

answer.actor: A student of Rabbi Eliezer
answer.event: A student of Rabbi Eliezer was liable to death by burning for sins against God.
answer.turn: The Rabbis said to leave him alone.
answer.outcome: He was spared because he had served a great person.
answer.summary: Rabbi Eliezer had a student who was liable to be burned for his sins against God. The Rabbis said to leave him alone because he had served a great man, and he was spared.
answer.missing: What the student did and how the matter came before the Rabbis; only the verdict is given.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Hama, Rabbi Afes and Levi
answer.event: Rabbi Hanina refused the appointment to head the yeshiva out of deference to the older Rabbi Afes, who took the seat while he and Levi studied outside.
answer.turn: Rabbi Afes died and Rabbi Hanina took the head seat, leaving Levi with no one to study with.
answer.outcome: Levi went to Babylonia, where Rav inferred these events from Levi's ruling.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi appointed Hanina bar Hama head of the yeshiva, but Hanina refused out of respect for Rabbi Afes, who was older. Afes sat at the head while Hanina sat outside with Levi. When Afes died, Hanina took the head seat and Levi had no one to study with, so he went to Babylonia, and Rav deduced all this when he heard of a limping scholar there.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman in her waiting period, and Rafram
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman within three months of her divorce or widowhood and fled.
answer.turn: The case came to Rafram.
answer.outcome: Rafram ruled that his flight was sufficient punishment.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman during the three months after her divorce or husband's death, which is forbidden, and then fled. When an incident like this came before Rafram, he said the man's flight was punishment enough and he was not excommunicated.
answer.missing: Who the man was and what led to the incident; the passage mostly states a dispute between Rav Aha and Rafram.

answer.actor: Rav Hisda, and a man who betrothed a woman with a blue stone
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone, and Rav Hisda appraised it and ruled on her status, rejecting a mother's objection.
answer.turn: The stone was no longer worth a peruta, and the man's mother objected that it had been worth that much on the day of betrothal.
answer.outcome: Rav Hisda answered that she cannot make the woman forbidden to a later man, and compared it to Yehudit and Rabbi Hiyya's mother-in-law-style claim.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a blue stone and Rav Hisda sat appraising it, ruling that if it was not worth a peruta she was not betrothed. The man's mother protested that it had been worth a peruta on the day of betrothal. Rav Hisda replied that she could not make the woman forbidden to a later suitor, and likened this to Yehudit, who tried to leave Rabbi Hiyya over a claim from her mother about her betrothal and was told her mother had no power to forbid her to him.
answer.missing: The stone episode is mostly a legal ruling with a brief exchange, and the ending of the Yehudit comparison is only sketched.

answer.actor: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, schoolteacher of Reish Lakish
answer.event: Rav Hiyya bar Adda was absent for three days and, asked why, said he had been harvesting from the one vine his father left him.
answer.turn: Each day's harvest of 300 clusters yielded less wine per cluster, and he gave away over half.
answer.outcome: Reish Lakish told him the yield would have been greater had he not interrupted the children's Torah study.
answer.summary: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, who taught Reish Lakish as a child, missed three days of teaching. When Reish Lakish asked why, he explained he had been harvesting one vine his father left him, 300 clusters a day, with each cluster filling a jug on day one, one jug per two clusters on day two, and per three on day three, and he gave away more than half. Reish Lakish replied that had he not been absent, the vine would have yielded even more.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua
answer.event: Asked about the rival wife of a daughter, Rabbi Yehoshua declined to rule between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
answer.turn: He said he feared the two great schools would break his skull, but offered testimony instead.
answer.outcome: He testified that two great Jerusalem families descended from rival wives, including High Priests, showing the practice.
answer.summary: People asked Rabbi Yehoshua about the rival wife of a daughter, and he said it was a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Pressed on whose view is law, he asked why they were putting his head between two great mountains, fearing they would crush his skull. Instead he testified that two great Jerusalem families descended from rival wives who remarried, and High Priests came from them.

answer.actor: Ravina
answer.event: Ravina, who held his orphan nephew's wine, asked Rav Ashi whether he could take it along with his own wine to Sikhra.
answer.turn: He was unsure whether to sell the orphan's wine at that time.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi told him to go, since the orphan's wine is no better than his own.
answer.summary: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphaned nephew, Ravina the younger, and also had wine of his own that he was taking to Sikhra to sell. He asked Rav Ashi whether he might bring the orphan's wine along. Rav Ashi told him to go, since the orphan's wine was no better than his own.

answer.actor: A blind man who reviewed mishnayot before Mar Shmuel
answer.event: The blind man was late, Mar Shmuel sent a messenger, the messenger missed him and returned reporting that the blind man's wife had committed adultery.
answer.turn: The blind man came to Mar Shmuel to ask whether he must heed this single report.
answer.outcome: Mar Shmuel told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not to if he did not.
answer.summary: A blind man who reviewed mishnayot before Mar Shmuel failed to show up one day, so Shmuel sent a messenger after him. They took different routes and missed each other, and the messenger went to the man's house and came back saying the man's wife had committed adultery. The blind man came to Shmuel, who told him: if you trust the messenger, divorce her; if not, do not.

answer.actor: A man who deposited silk, and Rabbi Abba
answer.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without saying anything, and the claimant came before Rabbi Abba.
answer.turn: No one knew whose the silk was after Rav Dimi died.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded it to the claimant because Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark, provided he did not regularly come and go there.
answer.summary: A man left silk in the house of Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without leaving instructions. The claimant came before Rabbi Abba, who ruled for him, since Rav Dimi was known not to be wealthy and the claimant described the silk, with the caveat that this holds only if he was not a regular visitor to the house.

answer.actor: A sharecropper
answer.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions taken from the field he worked and asked Rava about her status.
answer.turn: Rava asked who had relinquished the onions to him, implying they were stolen.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal fails for a handful, though a whole bundle would be fine since the sharecropper could say one bundle for another.
answer.summary: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field where he worked and came before Rava. Rava asked who had given him permission to take them, treating them as stolen so the woman was not betrothed. He added that if it had been a bundle, the sharecropper could have said he took one bundle and the owner may take one, since they split the crop anyway.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on his deathbed
answer.event: As he was dying, Rabbi named Babylonian places and their people, including one village that turned away after trapping fish on Shabbat and was excommunicated.
answer.turn: The Bireta DeSatya villagers desecrated Shabbat and became apostates after excommunication, while Adda bar Ahava is singled out.
answer.outcome: He says that today Adda bar Ahava, just circumcised, sits in Abraham's lap and Rav Yehuda was born in Babylonia.
answer.summary: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi described several Babylonian towns, such as one full of Ammonites and one of mamzerim, and one whose people trapped fish on Shabbat, were excommunicated by Rabbi Ahai, and became apostates. He then mentioned Adda bar Ahava, who that day was circumcised and sits in Abraham's lap, and said Rav Yehuda was born that day in Babylonia.
answer.missing: Mostly a list of statements rather than a sequence of events; only the fish-trapping episode is a small story.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef
answer.event: Two deeds on the same property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one only 'Nisan'.
answer.turn: The holder of the undated deed protested that he would lose.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef told him his deed could be from the twenty-ninth, so the property went to the specific date; when asked for authorization to repossess later sales, Rav Yosef noted the buyer could say his deed is from the first.
answer.summary: Two deeds for the same property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one just 'Nisan'. He awarded the property to the holder of the fifth of Nisan deed. The other protested, and Rav Yosef answered that his deed might be from the twenty-ninth. The man then asked for a document allowing him to repossess property sold from Iyyar on, and Rav Yosef said a purchaser could reply that his deed is from the first of Nisan.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with stolen dinars
answer.event: A man grabbed coins from another person, threw them to a woman washing her feet and declared her betrothed.
answer.turn: He then asked Rava whether she was betrothed.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled that the owner has not despaired of the money, so the stolen dinars were not his and the betrothal has no effect.
answer.summary: A woman was washing her feet in a basin when a man snatched dinars from someone else, threw them to her, and said she was betrothed to him. He later asked Rava about her status. Rava said the money was not truly the man's, since an owner is presumed not to have given up on stolen money, so the betrothal did nothing.

answer.actor: Rabba bar bar Hana and Rabbi Yochanan
answer.event: Rabba bar bar Hana recalls following Rabbi Yochanan to eat Genosar fruits, where Rabbi Yochanan would eat huge amounts.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yochanan then said he had not tasted something that nourishes, which seems to contradict the earlier ruling that fruit is nourishment.
answer.outcome: The Gemara corrects the wording to say he had not tasted sustaining food.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana recalled going with Rabbi Yochanan to eat the fruits of Genosar, where each person took ten or a hundred fruits and Rabbi Yochanan ate them all. He would then swear he had not tasted nourishment. The Gemara, finding this difficult, says the wording should be that he had not tasted sustaining food.
answer.missing: Habitual recollection told as a proof, not a single dated incident.

answer.actor: Reish Lakish
answer.event: Another presumptive-priest case came before Rabbi Yochanan while Reish Lakish and Rabbi Elazar sat there, and Reish Lakish demanded evidence that the man received a share at the threshing floor.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yochanan answered, 'And if there is no threshing floor, does priesthood cease?', the same line Rabbi Elazar had earlier said.
answer.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing the statement in Rabbi Yochanan's name.
answer.summary: Earlier, Rabbi Elazar had answered Reish Lakish's insistence on a threshing-floor share with the remark that priesthood does not cease if there is no threshing floor. Later, with the three sitting before Rabbi Yochanan, a similar case arose, Reish Lakish repeated his demand, and Rabbi Yochanan gave the same retort. Reish Lakish then looked sharply at Rabbi Elazar and complained that he had heard the teaching of Rabbi Yochanan and not told them it was in his name.

answer.actor: A couple who performed halitza in prison
answer.event: A couple performed halitza privately in prison and the case came before Rabbi Akiva, who validated it.
answer.turn: It is questioned how anyone could know what happened between them; witnesses saw from outside.
answer.outcome: Rav Yehuda says the incident and the case both took place in prison, and witnesses watched from outside.
answer.summary: A mishna tells of a couple who performed halitza alone in prison, a case that Rabbi Akiva validated. The Gemara asks how anyone knew what passed between them and answers that witnesses watched from outside. It then asks whether the act took place in prison or only came before Akiva there, concluding both were in prison.
answer.missing: The incident itself is only referred to from the mishna, not told in the segments shown; the passage is mostly discussion of it.

answer.actor: Rav Aha bar Yaakov
answer.event: Rav Aha bar Yaakov permitted the freed sons of Yudan the maidservant to marry each other's wives, and Rava objected that Rav Sheshet prohibited it.
answer.turn: Rava challenged him with Rav Sheshet's opposite ruling.
answer.outcome: Rav Aha replied that Rav Sheshet prohibited it and he permits it.
answer.summary: The sons of Yudan the maidservant were freed, and Rav Aha bar Yaakov permitted them to marry each other's wives. Rava objected that Rav Sheshet had forbidden this, and Rav Aha answered that Sheshet forbade it but he permits it.
answer.missing: A brief ruling and exchange, with no real development.

answer.actor: A creditor and the herdsman of orphans
answer.event: A creditor seized an ox from the herdsman of orphans, claiming he seized it during the debtor's life, while the herdsman said it was after death.
answer.turn: The herdsman had no witnesses that the creditor seized it from him.
answer.outcome: Rav Nachman ruled that since the creditor could simply claim he bought it, he is believed that he seized it during the debtor's life.
answer.summary: A creditor seized an ox from the herdsman of orphans, saying he did so while the debtor was alive, which would make it valid; the herdsman said it was after the debtor's death. They came before Rav Nachman, who asked the herdsman for witnesses and heard he had none. He ruled the creditor was believed, since he could have said he bought the ox.

answer.actor: Ulla and Rabbi Elazar
answer.event: Ulla, who often went up to Eretz Yisrael, died outside it, and Rabbi Elazar was told.
answer.turn: Rabbi Elazar quoted that he died in an unclean land, even though they said his coffin was coming to Eretz Yisrael.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Elazar said that being absorbed by the land after death is not like being absorbed while alive.
answer.summary: Ulla used to go up to Eretz Yisrael, but he died abroad. When told, Rabbi Elazar said Ulla had fulfilled the verse about dying in an unclean land. They answered that his coffin was being brought to Eretz Yisrael, and Rabbi Elazar replied that being taken in by the land after death is not the same as being taken in while alive.

answer.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef, son of Rava
answer.event: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava came before Rav Nechemya and asked for sustenance and then wine.
answer.turn: She asked for wine as well as sustenance.
answer.outcome: Rav Nechemya granted both, saying the people of Mechoza are known to drink wine.
answer.summary: The wife of Rav Yosef, son of Rava, came before Rav Nechemya and asked him to fix her sustenance, which he did. She then asked for wine, and he granted that too, explaining that the people of Mechoza are known to drink wine.

answer.actor: Mar Yehuda, Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel, and Rabba
answer.event: Mar Yehuda met Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel at Rabba's door and drew an inference from a baraita, then raised a contradiction from another.
answer.turn: They had no answer, and went to Rabba, who said a quarrelsome person had put them up to it.
answer.outcome: Rabba resolved it by saying the first baraita concerns an animal slaughtered and found a tereifa.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda found Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel at the door of Rabba's study hall and told them a baraita from which he inferred Rabbi Shimon holds the prohibition is not by Torah law. He then raised a contradiction from another baraita, and they were silent. They took the difficulty to Rabba, who said a troublemaker had set them up and resolved it by saying the first baraita deals with an animal slaughtered and found to be a tereifa.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, then Rabbi Hiyya
answer.event: Yehoshua ben Levi visited Gavla, saw calf-sized grape clusters and cursed the land for feeding gentiles; the next year Hiyya visited and saw goat-sized clusters.
answer.turn: The land shrank its produce in answer to the curse.
answer.outcome: The locals told Hiyya to go away and not do to them what his colleague did.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi came to Gavla and saw clusters of grapes as big as calves. He lamented that such fruit only fed the gentiles who ruled over Israel and told the earth to withhold it. The next year Rabbi Hiyya visited and saw clusters only as big as goats, and the locals told him to leave and not do to them what his colleague had done.

answer.actor: A man who had never been married, and Rav Nahman
answer.event: An unmarried man told Rav Nahman he had found an unobstructed orifice (non-virgin bride) on his wedding night.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman doubted how he could know without prior experience.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ordered him flogged with palm branches.
answer.summary: A man who had never been married came before Rav Nahman and claimed that his bride was not a virgin. Rav Nahman reasoned that a bachelor could only know this through experience with prostitutes, and ordered him flogged with palm branches.

answer.actor: Rafram and Rav Ashi
answer.event: Rafram pressured Rav Ashi into giving a firm ruling in a case, and Rav Ashi collected the full value.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi was pressured into an unequivocal ruling.
answer.outcome: He collected the full debt value, treating the damage like a beam for a sculpture.
answer.summary: There was a case like the one just discussed, and Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to rule firmly. Rav Ashi then had the claimant collect the full value of the document.
answer.missing: The facts of the incident itself (who, what was forgiven) are not told; it only gestures at a case.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel
answer.event: Funerals had become so costly that families abandoned the dead; Rabban Gamliel had himself taken out in plain linen.
answer.turn: His self-deprecating example changed the custom.
answer.outcome: Everyone followed, and today even rough cloth worth a zuz is used.
answer.summary: Funeral costs had become so burdensome that relatives would leave the dead and flee. Rabban Gamliel set an example by being buried in plain linen, and all the people followed him. Rav Pappa notes that today people bury the dead even in cheap rough cloth.

answer.actor: A dying man, Toviya, and Rabbi Yohanan
answer.event: A man declared his property should go to Toviya and died; Toviya came to claim it.
answer.turn: Possible doubt about which Toviya was meant.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that this Toviya has come and takes it.
answer.summary: A man told those present that his property should go to Toviya, then died. Toviya came to claim the estate, and Rabbi Yohanan said that Toviya had come, so there was no need to worry he meant someone else.

answer.actor: Shmuel, his father, and Shmuel's daughters
answer.event: Shmuel's father posted guards over captive women and Shmuel mocked it; later Shmuel's own daughters were captured and brought to Eretz Yisrael.
answer.turn: The daughters, leaving their captors outside, claimed purity before Rabbi Hanina's court and were permitted to marry priests; the captors then came.
answer.outcome: It was revealed they were Shmuel's daughters; their permitted status stood, and Rabbi Hanina told a priest to go marry one of them.
answer.summary: Shmuel's father posted guards over captive women brought to Neharde'a, and Shmuel questioned this. His father asked whether he would be so dismissive if they were his daughters. Later Shmuel's daughters were captured, left their captors outside and told Rabbi Hanina's court each that she was pure, and were permitted. Their captors then came in, the truth emerged, and Rabbi Hanina urged a priest to marry one of them.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa, Yehuda bar Mareimar, and Abba of Sura
answer.event: Rav Pappa went to write his son's marriage contract with Abba of Sura; Yehuda bar Mareimar met him but balked at entering the house, fearing his presence would pressure the father to give a larger dowry.
answer.turn: Rav Pappa pressed him to enter; his silent presence led Abba to write over everything he owned.
answer.outcome: Yehuda said he did not want even that much; Abba offered to retract and Yehuda said he should uphold his word, though it was not to his liking.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa went to Abba of Sura's house to arrange his son's marriage contract, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came to greet him but hesitated at the door. Rav Pappa pressed him in and he sat in silence. Abba thought he was angry and wrote all his property into the dowry. Yehuda said he did not want that, and Abba offered to retract, but Yehuda said he should not become a man who retracts his word.

answer.actor: Rava
answer.event: Rava taught that one may scatter straw in a rain-damaged courtyard on Shabbat; Rav Pappa challenged him with a baraita.
answer.turn: Rava realized his ruling was wrong.
answer.outcome: He had a spokesman publicly announce his error and corrected the ruling.
answer.summary: Rava taught that one may scatter straw in a rain-damaged courtyard on Shabbat. Rav Pappa objected from a baraita requiring a special manner. Rava then appointed a spokesman and publicly declared that his earlier statement was a mistake and gave the corrected rule.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hiyya and Bar Kappara
answer.event: The two disputed whether a person is liable on two counts or one in several cases, and each leaped up and swore by the Temple service that he had heard his view from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
answer.turn: Contradictory oaths, so each argued logically.
answer.outcome: Not resolved by narrative; later the Gemara speculates Bar Kappara mixed up cases.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hiyya and Bar Kappara disagreed on whether a non-priest serving on Shabbat is liable twice or once. Each leaped up and swore by the Temple service that he had heard his answer from Rabbi. They then reasoned it through, and repeated the same dispute and oaths for two more cases.
answer.missing: No real ending; most of the passage is legal analysis of why they differed.

answer.actor: A man sent by his father to fetch chicks
answer.event: A man climbed to a roof at his father's command, sent away the mother bird and took the young, and fell and died on the way back.
answer.turn: He died despite fulfilling two mitzvot with promised long life.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yaakov took this as evidence reward is in the world to come.
answer.summary: A father told his son to climb to the roof and fetch chicks. The son sent away the mother bird and took the young, fulfilling both honoring a parent and the mother bird mitzva, but on his return he fell and died.
answer.missing: The passage shown [4]-[6] only argues about this incident; the story itself is in the preceding context segment.

answer.actor: A man claiming another is a priest, and Rabbi Ami
answer.event: A man came to Rabbi Ami saying another man had established presumptive status as a priest because he read first in the synagogue.
answer.turn: Rabbi Ami questioned whether he read first as a priest or as a great man; the man answered a Levite read after him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood on his word.
answer.summary: A man came before Rabbi Ami and said that another man was a presumptive priest because he read first in the synagogue. Rabbi Ami asked whether that was due to priesthood or prominence, and the man replied that a Levite read after him. Rabbi Ami then elevated him to priesthood on that testimony.

answer.actor: A man drinking wine and a woman who asked him for a cup
answer.event: A woman asked a man in a shop for a cup of wine; he asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it.
answer.turn: She answered only with a repeated demand to give her a drink, not agreeing.
answer.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that such an answer is nothing and she is not betrothed.
answer.summary: A man was drinking wine in a store when a woman asked him for a cup. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she answered only by repeating her request to be given a drink. Rav Hama ruled that this was meaningless and she was not betrothed.

answer.actor: Mar Yehuda and Rava
answer.event: Mar Yehuda found the residents of Mavrakhta placing their eruvin at the entrance of a synagogue and told them to place them farther in to gain more distance.
answer.turn: Rava reacted dismissively, calling him argumentative and saying no one follows Rabbi Akiva on this.
answer.outcome: Rava rejected Mar Yehuda's advice as following a discarded opinion.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda found people from Mavrakhta placing their eruvin in a synagogue and told them to put them farther in so more would be permitted to them. Rava called him argumentative and said nobody follows Rabbi Akiva's opinion on this, since the halakha follows the Rabbis.

answer.actor: A man who rented a donkey, and the owner
answer.event: The owner told the renter to avoid the Pekod River road where there was water; the renter took that road and the donkey died.
answer.turn: The renter claimed there was no water and the death had another cause.
answer.outcome: Rava accepted his claim on the principle of why would I lie, though Abaye objected that this does not apply where witnesses know there is water.
answer.summary: A man rented out a donkey and warned the renter not to take the river road. The renter went that way and the donkey died. He came before Rava and admitted going that way but said there was no water, and Rava accepted his claim since he could have lied. Abaye objected that the principle fails when the facts are known.

answer.actor: An Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael
answer.event: The Amorite asked how much the resident gathers from a palm tree on the Jordan bank.
answer.turn: The Amorite jeered that Israel had already ruined the land since they got 120 kor.
answer.outcome: The resident retorted he had only spoken of one side of the tree.
answer.summary: An Amorite asked a resident of Eretz Yisrael how much fruit he took from a palm tree by the Jordan, and he said sixty kor. The Amorite scoffed that they got 120 and Israel had already ruined the land. The Israelite replied that he was speaking of only one side of the tree.

answer.actor: A debtor, his creditor, and the purchaser of his land
answer.event: A debtor owing 100 sold two plots for 50 each; the creditor repossessed one from a purchaser and then came to repossess the other.
answer.turn: The second purchaser took 100 dinars to the creditor and offered a choice.
answer.outcome: Not told in the passage; the creditor's response is not shown.
answer.summary: A man owed a creditor 100 dinars and sold two plots of land for 50 each. The creditor repossessed one, then came for the other. The second purchaser took 100 dinars to him and said: if the plot is worth 100 to you fine, otherwise take the 100 and give up your claim on both plots.
answer.missing: How the creditor responded; the ending is not narrated.

answer.actor: A blind man who reviewed mishnayot before Mar Shmuel
answer.event: The blind man was late, Mar Shmuel sent a messenger who missed him on the road and then reported that the blind man's wife had committed adultery.
answer.turn: The blind man, who had not been at home, had to decide what to do on the word of a single messenger.
answer.outcome: Mar Shmuel told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not to if he did not.
answer.summary: A blind man who studied mishnayot with Mar Shmuel one day failed to arrive. Mar Shmuel sent a messenger after him. The two took different roads and missed each other, and the messenger reached the man's house. The messenger came back and said the man's wife had committed adultery. The blind man brought this to Mar Shmuel, who told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger and not to if he did not.

answer.actor: A man who came before Rabban Gamliel
answer.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel he had found an unobstructed orifice on his wedding night.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested he had approached from a different angle and told a parable of a man groping in the dark who finds a door open only if he diverts.
answer.outcome: Rabban Gamliel did not accept the claim at face value and offered his parable as the explanation (a second version has him say the man diverted deliberately).
answer.summary: A man came before Rabban Gamliel and said he had found his bride's passage open. Rabban Gamliel asked whether he had approached from the wrong angle, and told him a parable: a man walking in the dark finds a door open if he pushes aside what blocks it, and locked if he does not. Some say instead that he asked whether the man had deliberately displaced the door and bolt.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa
answer.event: Rav Pappa served drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding and poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, who did not stand before him.
answer.turn: Rav Pappa was offended that he was not shown the respect due to him.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
answer.summary: At the wedding of his son Abba Mar, Rav Pappa was serving the guests drinks. When he poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, Rav Yitzhak did not stand up for him, and Rav Pappa became angry.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives
answer.event: They seized an orphans' cow from an alley over a debt and asked Rabbi Yohanan, who approved.
answer.turn: Reish Lakish told them to return the cow, and they went back to Rabbi Yohanan.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he could do nothing, since a colleague of his stature disagreed with him.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized an orphans' cow in an alley and Rabbi Yohanan told them they had seized it properly. They then went to Reish Lakish, who told them to give it back. They returned to Rabbi Yohanan, who said that since his equal disagreed with him he could not help them.

answer.actor: A woman selling belts
answer.event: A man snatched a belt from her and, when she asked for it back, asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it.
answer.turn: She took the belt and said nothing.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled she could say she merely took her own property, so her silence did not make a betrothal.
answer.summary: A woman was selling belts when a man snatched one. She asked for it back and he asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it. She took it and stayed silent. Rav Nahman ruled that she could say she had only taken her own property, so no betrothal resulted.

answer.actor: Mar Yehuda, Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel, and Rabba
answer.event: Mar Yehuda met two colleagues at the study hall entrance and raised a proof from one baraita, then a contradiction from another.
answer.turn: They had no answer and fell silent.
answer.outcome: They brought the difficulty to Rabba, who dismissed it as the work of a quarrelsome person and resolved it by explaining the first baraita as dealing with an animal found to be a tereifa.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda found Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel at the door of Rabba's study hall and cited a baraita from which he drew an inference about Rabbi Shimon. He then raised a second baraita that contradicted it, and they could not answer. They went to Rabba, who said a quarrelsome person had put them up to it and resolved the contradiction by limiting the first baraita to an animal found to be a tereifa.

answer.actor: Rav Giddel and Rabbi Abba
answer.event: Rav Giddel was negotiating to buy a plot of land and Rabbi Abba bought it first; Rav Giddel complained through Rabbi Zeira to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha.
answer.turn: Rav Yitzhak Nappaha confronted Rabbi Abba with a parable of a pauper whose loaf is taken, and Rabbi Abba said he had not known.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Abba refused to sell it but offered it as a gift; Rav Giddel would not take a gift and Rabbi Abba would not take the land, so it was called the land of the Sages.
answer.summary: Rav Giddel was working to buy a plot when Rabbi Abba bought it. The complaint went from Rav Giddel to Rabbi Zeira to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, who confronted Rabbi Abba at the festival. Rabbi Abba said he had not known and would not sell, since it was his first purchase, but would give it as a gift. Rav Giddel refused a gift and Rabbi Abba would not keep the land, so it became known as the land of the Sages.

answer.actor: A yavam and yevama who both admitted no levirate marriage was consummated
answer.event: They came before Rava, who ordered halitza for her.
answer.turn: Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires both a bill of divorce and halitza.
answer.outcome: Rava retracted his ruling on account of the baraita.
answer.summary: A couple, a yavam and yevama, both admitted they had not consummated the levirate marriage and came before Rava. Rava told the Sages to arrange halitza for her. Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires a bill of divorce as well as halitza, and Rava answered that if it is taught, it is taught, retracting his ruling.

answer.actor: A husband who collected his wife's inheritance, and Rabbi Ami
answer.event: A man travelled with six hundred of his own dinars to collect his wife's four hundred in Bei Hozai and took one dinar of hers on the way back.
answer.turn: The Rabbis objected to Rabbi Ami's ruling that the man had spent his money and eaten hers, saying he had consumed principal rather than produce.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami replied that this made him one who spent and did not eat, who swears to what he spent and collects it.
answer.summary: A woman inherited four hundred dinars in Bei Hozai. Her husband went and brought it back at a cost of six hundred of his own dinars, and used one dinar of hers on the way. Rabbi Ami ruled that what he spent and what he ate cancel out. The Rabbis objected that he had eaten principal, and Rabbi Ami answered that then he was one who spent without eating and may swear and collect his expenses.

answer.actor: A maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household
answer.event: She immersed in a ritual bath, and on coming out a bone was found between her teeth.
answer.turn: The foreign object in her mouth put the validity of her immersion in doubt.
answer.outcome: Rabbi required her to immerse again.
answer.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi's household immersed herself ritually. When she came up, a bone was found between her teeth. Rabbi had her immerse a second time.
answer.missing: The incident is cited only as an objection in a legal argument.

answer.actor: A groom and bride before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
answer.event: The groom said he found no blood, and the bride said she was a virgin.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel had the cloth brought, soaked and laundered it, and found drops of blood on it.
answer.outcome: He told the groom to go take possession of his acquisition.
answer.summary: A man came before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi and said he had found no blood on his wedding night, while his bride said she had been a virgin. Rabban Gamliel asked for the cloth, soaked it in water and washed it, and found drops of blood on it. He told the groom to go and take possession of his bride.

answer.actor: Rav Yehuda
answer.event: A narrow inlet of the sea breached a courtyard wall in a shepherds' village and the matter came before Rav Yehuda.
answer.turn: The case seemed to conflict with Shmuel's other ruling requiring a majority of the wall or two boards.
answer.outcome: Rav Yehuda required only one upright board to remain in order to permit the courtyard.
answer.summary: In a shepherds' village an inlet of the sea cut through a courtyard and breached a whole wall. The case came before Rav Yehuda, who required only one standing board of wall to permit the courtyard. Rav Yosef cites this to Abaye, who answers that water is treated leniently.
answer.missing: The incident is told briefly as a precedent in an argument.

answer.actor: Ameimar
answer.event: A woman came before Ameimar asking for one-tenth of her father's estate, and her brothers said that if they had the money they would pay her off.
answer.turn: Ameimar stayed silent at that.
answer.outcome: Rav Minyumi took his silence to show that Ameimar had retracted and treated the daughter as a creditor who can be paid in cash.
answer.summary: Rav Minyumi was standing before Ameimar when a woman came asking for her one-tenth share of her father's estate. Her brothers said that if they had money they would pay her off. Ameimar said nothing, and Rav Minyumi took this to mean that Ameimar had retracted and now saw her as a creditor.
answer.missing: The passage opens with Rav Ashi's opinion; the incident is cited as proof.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin (or Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Zevida, or Ameimar)
answer.event: A visiting sage ruled on the children of a slave and a Jewish woman, once for an unmarried woman and once for a married woman.
answer.turn: Rav Sheshet gave a different account of who ruled and how.
answer.outcome: The reports conflict and the Gemara then states the law as fit in both cases.
answer.summary: Ravina reports that when Rabbi Yosei bar Avin visited a town, he ruled the child of a slave and an unmarried woman fit and that of a married woman unfit. Rav Sheshet says it was another Rabbi Yosei who ruled both fit, and Rav Aha reports that Ameimar also ruled both fit.
answer.missing: These are conflicting reports of rulings with no scene or detail, so there is no real story.

answer.actor: Rav
answer.event: Rav arrived at Apsetaya and prohibited climbing even a tree stripped of its branches.
answer.turn: This seemed to contradict the permission just stated.
answer.outcome: The Gemara explains Rav found an unguarded field and fenced it in as a safeguard.
answer.summary: Rav arrived in Apsetaya and forbade people to climb even a stripped tree. The Gemara says he found an unguarded field, meaning widespread transgression, and put a fence around it.
answer.missing: It is a one-line precedent cited against a rule, with no scene or characters beyond Rav.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman
answer.event: Rav Nahman found Rav Adda bar Ahava and his son-in-law Rav Hana in the Pumbedita marketplace posing challenges to each other about the mishna.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman told them he thought even the deaf-mute brother's widow was uncertain.
answer.outcome: He gave his own view and the exchange ends there.
answer.summary: Rav Nahman came upon Rav Adda bar Ahava and his son-in-law Rav Hana sitting in the Pumbedita marketplace debating a mishna. They explained their limit for the rule and Rav Nahman answered that even in the deaf-mute brother's case it was still uncertain.
answer.missing: The setting is a framing for a legal debate, with no event beyond the conversation.

answer.actor: Mar Ukva and his wife
answer.event: Mar Ukva secretly tossed four dinars daily into a poor neighbor's doorway, and one day the poor man tried to catch the giver.
answer.turn: The poor man chased them, and the couple fled into a still-hot furnace, scorching Mar Ukva's feet while his wife was unharmed.
answer.outcome: His wife told him to rest his feet on hers, and when he was distraught she explained her giving was more immediate because she gave food at home.
answer.summary: Mar Ukva daily slipped four dinars into a poor neighbor's door slot. One day the poor man went to see who his benefactor was, and Mar Ukva and his wife, who came together that day, ran from him into a furnace with banked embers. Mar Ukva's feet were burned, and his wife offered her unburned feet to rest on. When he was upset, she explained that her help was greater because she gave immediate food at home.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman
answer.event: A woman from Mehoza married to a man of Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman, who recognized her accent.
answer.turn: He first ruled by Babylonian custom, then the litigants objected that she was marrying into Neharde'a.
answer.outcome: He reversed to rule that Neharde'a and its towns follow Shmuel.
answer.summary: A woman from Mehoza, married to a man from Neharde'a, came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract. He heard her accent and ruled that Babylonia follows Rav. When they objected that she was marrying into Neharde'a, he said that in that case Neharde'a and its towns follow Shmuel.
answer.missing: What the exact dispute about her contract was is only in context.

answer.actor: The sister of Rami bar Hama and her husband Rav Avya
answer.event: Her marriage contract was lost and the couple asked Rav Yosef what to do.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef cited the lenient view that a man may keep his wife for years without a contract, and Abaye objected that the law follows Rabbi Meir's stringency.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef conceded and said to go and write her a new contract.
answer.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister, married to Rav Avya, lost her marriage contract, and the couple went to Rav Yosef. He first said the stringent view is Rabbi Meir's and the Rabbis allow years without a contract. Abaye objected that the law follows Rabbi Meir, so Rav Yosef told the husband to write her a new contract.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abbahu
answer.event: A marriage contract was brought before Rabbi Abbahu, with the scribe's handwriting and one witness's signature recognized.
answer.turn: Rabbi Abbahu was ready to validate it, but Rabbi Yirmeya said the mishna requires the scribe to have signed.
answer.outcome: The implication is that the contract is not validated on those grounds.
answer.summary: A marriage contract came before Rabbi Abbahu, with the scribe's writing and one witness's signature recognized. He was inclined to accept it. Rabbi Yirmeya told him the mishna means the scribe must have signed as a witness, so the handwriting alone is not enough.
answer.missing: The final decision is not explicitly stated.

answer.actor: Rava and Rav Mari bar Rahel
answer.event: Rava declared Rav Mari bar Rahel, son of a gentile father and Jewish mother, fit and appointed him an official in Babylonia.
answer.turn: A verse seems to require officials to come from among 'your brethren', but Rava reasoned that a Jewish mother suffices.
answer.outcome: Rav Mari was appointed.
answer.summary: Rava ruled that Rav Mari bar Rahel, whose mother was Jewish and father a gentile, was fit and appointed him one of Babylonia's officials. Despite the verse limiting appointments to your brethren, Rava held that a Jewish mother makes him count as one.
answer.missing: This is mainly a ruling with its justification; there is little scene or detail.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
answer.event: They planned to let a nursing mother remarry immediately, following a baraita.
answer.turn: An old woman said Rav Nahman had forbidden it to her, and Rav Pappi cited a baraita of Rabbi Meir's decree.
answer.outcome: They admitted they had forgotten the principle, and the halakha was fixed with distinctions.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna were about to permit a woman to remarry quickly after her child was weaned or placed with a nurse. An old woman said Rav Nahman had forbidden it in her own case, and Rav Pappi showed them a baraita requiring a wait. They said they had forgotten, and the ruling was set with distinctions.
answer.missing: Mostly legal argument; the narrative is thin and its end is a ruling.

answer.actor: Rav Yehuda bar Yehezkel and Rav Nahman
answer.event: A man from Neharde'a insulted Rav Yehuda at a Pumbedita butcher shop, so Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and declared him a slave, and the man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Nahman's court.
answer.turn: At Rav Nahman's house, Rav Yehuda used Shmuel's teachings to rebuke every courtesy Rav Nahman offered, until Yalta urged her husband to end it.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman accepted the case, questioned Rav Yehuda, and the litigant's claim of Hasmonean descent was refuted by Rav Mattana's testimony of Shmuel; the man was publicized as a slave, marriage contracts were torn, and a mob chasing Rav Yehuda dropped its stones when he threatened to reveal their lineages.
answer.summary: A man from Neharde'a insulted Rav Yehuda at a butcher shop and was excommunicated and declared a slave. He summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Nahman's court, and Rav Yehuda went and used Shmuel's teachings to correct every courtesy and word Rav Nahman offered. Rav Nahman then heard the case, and Rav Mattana confirmed Rav Yehuda's claim that anyone claiming Hasmonean descent is a slave. Many marriages were annulled, and when a mob pursued Rav Yehuda to stone him, he threatened to reveal their lineages and they dropped their stones.

answer.actor: Rav and Rav Yehuda
answer.event: The two were walking along a road with a woman ahead of them.
answer.turn: Rav told Rav Yehuda to hurry away from Gehenna, and Rav Yehuda pointed out Rav's own ruling that fit men may be secluded.
answer.outcome: Rav explained he meant only men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues, so they must still avoid it.
answer.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were walking and a woman walked ahead of them. Rav told Rav Yehuda to lift his feet away from Gehenna to avoid being secluded with her. Rav Yehuda reminded him that he had permitted this for fit men, and Rav replied that he meant only the likes of Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues, not them.

answer.actor: Ravina and Rav Ashi
answer.event: Ravina, sitting before Rav Ashi, saw a man tying his donkey to a tree on Shabbat and protested.
answer.turn: The man ignored him, so Ravina asked Rav Ashi to have him excommunicated, then worried that he had acted disrespectfully before his teacher.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi reassured him that where God's name is desecrated, one does not defer to a teacher.
answer.summary: Ravina was sitting before Rav Ashi when he saw a man tie his donkey to a tree on Shabbat. He called out to him but was ignored, and then said the man should be excommunicated. Afterward he asked whether this had seemed irreverent to Rav Ashi, who replied that when God's name is desecrated, no deference is owed to a teacher.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags, and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examined whether it was worth a peruta.
answer.turn: The rule that betrothal depends on the item's value seemed to conflict with Shmuel's concern that it might be worth a peruta elsewhere.
answer.outcome: The conflict is resolved by distinguishing certain from doubtful betrothal.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags, and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya sat before Rav and checked whether it was worth a peruta. If it was, she was betrothed; if not, she was not. This is then reconciled with Shmuel's view by distinguishing certain from uncertain betrothal.
answer.missing: What was decided about this particular woman is not stated.

answer.actor: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan
answer.event: They were walking on a road outside Eretz Yisrael and saw a man planting diverse seeds together, and another planting wheat and barley between grapevines.
answer.turn: One suggested ostracizing the man each time, but the other said the law was not clear to him.
answer.outcome: The other explained why the man's act was not clearly forbidden outside Eretz Yisrael, so no one was ostracized.
answer.summary: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan were traveling when they saw a man sowing mixed seeds. One proposed ostracizing him, and the other told him he did not understand the law. They then saw another man sowing wheat and barley among vines, and the same suggestion drew the reply that by Rabbi Yoshiya's view this is not yet a violation.

answer.actor: Rabbi Nehemya, Rava, and the poor men who came to them
answer.event: A man seeking charity told Rabbi Nehemya he usually dined on fatty meat and aged wine, and Rabbi Nehemya invited him to eat lentils; another man told Rava he ate fattened hen and aged wine.
answer.turn: The first man ate lentils and died; the second justified his food as coming from God, and just then Rava's sister arrived with a fattened hen and aged wine.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Nehemya blamed the man for pampering himself, and Rava told the second man to arise and eat.
answer.summary: A man asked Rabbi Nehemya for charity and said he normally ate fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemya asked him to share lentils, and the man died from the plain food. Rava heard a similar claim from another man, who said his food came from God, and then Rava's sister arrived with a fattened hen and aged wine. Rava said he had been answered and told the man to eat.

answer.actor: A woman who gave her property to her daughter, Rav Nahman, Rav Anan and Mar Ukva
answer.event: A woman wrote a gift of her property to her daughter to keep it from her future husband, was later divorced, and came before Rav Nahman to reclaim it.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman tore the document, Rav Anan complained to Mar Ukva, and Mar Ukva said Shmuel would tear such documents.
answer.outcome: Rava questioned Rav Nahman, who explained that even for her daughter the woman had not wholeheartedly given up her own interests.
answer.summary: A woman about to remarry wrote her property over to her daughter to keep it from her husband, and after she was divorced she wanted it back. Rav Nahman tore up the deed, and Rav Anan complained to Mar Ukva, who explained that Shmuel would tear such a document of evasion. Rava asked Rav Nahman his reason, and he said she would put her own interests before her daughter's.

answer.actor: Residents of a crooked alleyway in Sura and Rav Hisda
answer.event: The residents rolled up a mat and placed it at the turn of the alley to serve as a side post.
answer.turn: Rav Hisda said this was not valid by either Rav or Shmuel since the wind throws it down.
answer.outcome: The mat is declared ineffective unless pegged in.
answer.summary: The residents of a crooked alley in Sura put a rolled mat at its turn to permit carrying. Rav Hisda said this satisfied neither Rav nor Shmuel, since the wind blows the mat over and it counts as nothing.
answer.missing: The aftermath for the residents is not given; it is mostly a legal ruling on a case.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and two claimants holding deeds to the same field
answer.event: Two deeds to the same property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and the other only 'Nisan'.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef awarded the property to the dated deed, and the other man protested, asked for a document, and was told a buyer could claim his deed was from the first of Nisan.
answer.outcome: The remedy given is for the two to write authorizations for each other.
answer.summary: Two deeds to the same field came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and the other just 'Nisan'. He awarded the field to the dated one. The other man protested and asked for a document allowing him to repossess from later buyers, and Rav Yosef said buyers could claim his deed dated from the first of Nisan. The solution was for each to write the other an authorization.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: He went to learn Torah from Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua.
answer.turn: Elazar's students ganged up on him like the roosters of Beit Bukya and would not let him study.
answer.outcome: He learned only one teaching of Rabbi Eliezer, that one is liable to stoning for intercourse with a hermaphrodite as with a male.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi went to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua. The students there crowded in against him like fighting roosters and would not let him learn. All he managed to learn was one point of Rabbi Eliezer on stoning for intercourse with a hermaphrodite.
answer.missing: The framing quotation of Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is mixed into the same segment.

answer.actor: Rabbi Ami and a man claiming another man is a priest
answer.event: A man came before Rabbi Ami asserting that another man had established a presumption of priesthood, because he was called first to read the Torah.
answer.turn: Rabbi Ami asked whether the first reading reflected priesthood or mere prominence, and the man answered that a Levite read after him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami accepted the statement and elevated the man to the priesthood.
answer.summary: A man came before Rabbi Ami and said another man had shown himself to be a priest by reading the Torah first in the synagogue. Rabbi Ami asked whether he read first because he was a priest or because he was a great man. The witness answered that a Levite read after him, which only happens when a priest reads first. Rabbi Ami accepted this and elevated the man to the priesthood.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and a man vouching for another's Levite status
answer.event: A man came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi claiming another man was a Levite because he was called to read second in the synagogue.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi pressed whether second reading showed Levite status or mere prominence, and the man answered that a priest had read before him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accepted the statement and elevated the man to Levite status.
answer.summary: A man came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and said another man was shown to be a Levite because he read second in the synagogue. Rabbi Yehoshua asked whether that was because of Levite status or because of prominence. The man replied that he was certain, since a priest had read before him. Rabbi Yehoshua accepted this and elevated the man to Levite status.

answer.actor: Rav Amram the Pious
answer.event: Captive women redeemed in Neharde'a were lodged in Rav Amram's upper room with the ladder removed, and he was seized by desire for one of them and climbed a huge ladder alone.
answer.turn: Halfway up he stopped himself and cried out that there was a fire in Amram's house, bringing the Sages to see him.
answer.outcome: He said it was better to be shamed in this world than the next, adjured his evil inclination to leave him as a pillar of fire, and told it that he, flesh, was greater than it, fire.
answer.summary: Captive women who had been redeemed were put up in Rav Amram the Pious's house, with the ladder removed from their attic. One was so beautiful that light seemed to shine from the opening, and Rav Amram, desiring her, lifted a ladder ten men could not carry and began to climb. Halfway up he braced himself and cried out that there was a fire in his house, so the Sages came and saw him. He told them it was better to be shamed in this world, then made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire and declared that flesh had beaten fire.

answer.actor: Ameimar and a woman claiming one-tenth of her father's estate
answer.event: A woman came before Ameimar asking for a tenth of her father's estate, and her brothers said that if they had cash they would pay her off with it.
answer.turn: Ameimar stayed silent rather than objecting to the brothers' offer.
answer.outcome: Rav Minyumi took the silence to show Ameimar had retracted and now saw the daughter as a creditor who can be paid in money.
answer.summary: Rav Minyumi recalled standing before Ameimar when a woman came asking for a tenth of her father's estate. Her brothers said that if they had the money they would pay her off in cash, and Ameimar said nothing. Rav Minyumi read this silence as Ameimar's retraction of his earlier view.
answer.missing: The passage is mostly a legal dispute with the anecdote serving as evidence; no actual ruling in the woman's case is given.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman, judging between a creditor and a herdsman of orphans' cattle
answer.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman, claiming he took it while the debtor was alive, while the herdsman said it was after death.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman asked the herdsman for witnesses that the creditor seized it, and he had none.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman reasoned that since the creditor could claim he purchased it, he could equally claim he seized it during the debtor's life, so the creditor's claim stands.
answer.summary: A creditor seized an ox from the herdsman of some orphans, saying he took it while the father was alive. The herdsman said it was after the father's death, and they came before Rav Nahman. Rav Nahman asked the herdsman whether he had witnesses to the seizure, and he said no. Rav Nahman reasoned that the creditor could just as well have claimed to have bought the ox, so he is believed that he seized it during the debtor's lifetime.

answer.actor: Rava and Rav Natan bar Ami
answer.event: Rava coerced the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity and collected four hundred dinars from him.
answer.outcome: Rava collected four hundred dinars for charity from him against his will.
answer.summary: Rava once compelled the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami to give to charity and took four hundred dinars from him. It is cited as proof that a wealthy man can be forced to give, and so can be forced to support his children.
answer.missing: No detail of how the incident unfolded or Rav Natan's reaction; it is a one-line precedent.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yohanan
answer.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, who had to pay daily medical costs for their father's widow, asked him what to do, and he told them to fix a lump sum with the doctor.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan later regretted it, saying they had made themselves like legal advisors.
answer.outcome: The text explains he first followed the verse about not hiding from one's own flesh but concluded an important person should not do this.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had their father's wife on their hands, needing treatment every day. They came to him and he advised them to fix a lump sum with the doctor, which would turn the cost into a deduction from her marriage contract. Later he said in regret that they had made themselves like legal advisors, since at first he had thought it right to help relatives but ultimately held that an important person should not.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rava and his father Rava
answer.event: Rava sent his son Rav Yosef to study with Rav Yosef for six years, and on the eve of Yom Kippur after three years the son decided to go home to see his wife.
answer.turn: Rava heard, took a weapon and went to meet him, rebuking him for remembering his mistress or dove.
answer.outcome: Father and son were so upset by the argument that neither ate the pre-Yom Kippur meal.
answer.summary: Rava sent his son Rav Yosef to study for six years in the study hall. Three years in, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the son said he would go see his family. Rava heard, took a weapon and went out to meet him, asking whether he had remembered his mistress, or by another version his dove. They were so preoccupied by the clash that neither ate the cessation meal.

answer.actor: The court of priests
