answer.turn: Reish Lakish asked whether he had seen him take a share of terumah at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar objected that priesthood does not cease where there is no threshing floor.
answer.outcome: On a later occasion Reish Lakish realized Elazar was repeating Rabbi Yohanan's ruling and rebuked him for not saying so.
answer.summary: A man came before Reish Lakish claiming another was a priest because he had been called to read first in the synagogue. Reish Lakish demanded to know whether he had seen him get terumah at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar protested that there might be no threshing floor. Later, when Rabbi Yohanan said the same thing, Reish Lakish glared at Elazar for not saying it was Yohanan's ruling.
answer.missing: The first case's outcome is not stated, and the sequel is in the following context segment rather than the passage.

answer.actor: Rav Shimi bar Hiyya and Rav
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags, and Rav Shimi sat before Rav and appraised whether it was worth a peruta.
answer.turn: The Gemara notes that if it was not worth a peruta she would not be betrothed, which seems to contradict Shmuel, and resolves it as certain versus uncertain betrothal.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags. Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, sitting before Rav, examined it to see if it was worth a peruta: if yes she was betrothed, if not she was not.
answer.missing: No result of the examination is reported; the incident is a vehicle for a legal distinction.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hanina, his wife, and a pauper
answer.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his wife with the four dinars he gave a pauper every Shabbat eve.
answer.turn: She came back saying the man did not need it, because she heard people in his house asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hanina answered that we should be grateful to swindlers, since without them we would sin daily by not giving to the truly poor.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent a pauper four dinars every Friday afternoon. One day his wife took it and returned saying the man didn't need it, since she heard him being asked whether he ate off silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina responded with Rabbi Elazar's saying that we should thank swindlers, for without them we would sin every day.
answer.missing: It is not said whether Rabbi Hanina went on giving the money.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi
answer.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi, who prayed to be saved from the evil inclination, was approached by his wife in disguise as the prostitute Haruta while he studied in his garden.
answer.turn: He propositioned her and fetched the pomegranate she demanded; at home he found his wife lighting the oven and sat in it, and she revealed it had been she.
answer.outcome: He said he had still intended to transgress, and fasted for the rest of his life until he died.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi always prayed to be saved from the evil inclination, and his wife wondered why when he had long since withdrawn from her. One day she dressed up and passed him in his garden, calling herself Haruta. He propositioned her, climbed to get the pomegranate she asked for, and they lay together. At home he sat in the burning oven in shame; she told him it was she, but since he had intended a sin he fasted until he died.

answer.actor: Rav Rehumi and his wife
answer.event: Rav Rehumi, who studied before Rava, used to come home every Yom Kippur eve but one year got caught up in his study.
answer.turn: His wife waited, saying now he is coming, and a tear fell from her eye when he did not come.
answer.outcome: At that moment the roof he was sitting on collapsed and he died.
answer.summary: Rav Rehumi studied away from home and came back each Yom Kippur eve. One year he was absorbed in a halakha and did not come, while his wife kept waiting and finally shed a tear. At that very moment the roof he was sitting on gave way beneath him and he died.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef
answer.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave immersed a gentile woman for the sake of relations, and Rav Yosef said he could render her and her daughter fit.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave immersed a gentile woman, intending only to permit relations. Rav Yosef declared that he could treat both her and her daughter as fit to marry into Israel.
answer.missing: It is a case plus a ruling; no consequences or ending are told.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel
answer.event: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba, who died childless, and Rabban Gamliel entered levirate marriage with her rival wife.
answer.outcome: The Gemara then rejects the incident as a proof because she was an aylonit.
answer.summary: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba, who died without children. Rabban Gamliel then took Abba's other wife in levirate marriage. The Gemara questions whether this proves anything, since Rabban Gamliel followed Beit Hillel.
answer.missing: It is cited as legal evidence in one sentence, with no development.

answer.actor: A brewer
answer.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from beer he was making for someone else.
answer.turn: The owner found him and said why not give her from the sharper sediment, and the brewer asked Rava whether this meant the owner had relinquished it.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled the owner spoke only out of embarrassment, so the sediment was not given up and she was not betrothed.
answer.summary: A brewer making date beer for another man betrothed a woman using sediment from it. The owner came upon him and said he should have used the sharper sediment instead. The brewer asked Rava whether that meant the owner had agreed, and Rava answered that the owner spoke only out of embarrassment, so the woman was not betrothed.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon and his students
answer.event: While Rabbi Yehuda and others sat before Rabbi Tarfon, a yevama came to perform halitza.
answer.turn: Rabbi Tarfon told everyone to answer three times 'He who had his shoe removed'.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled sitting with others before Rabbi Tarfon when a yevama came to perform halitza. Rabbi Tarfon told them all to respond three times, 'He who had his shoe removed.'
answer.missing: It is a short recollection serving as a legal precedent, with no turn or ending.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
answer.event: Yeimar bar Hashu's agent seized a boat left by a dead debtor, and Rav Pappa and Rav Huna told him he cannot seize assets to the harm of other creditors.
answer.turn: Being creditors themselves, the two seized the boat, each declaring he had acquired all of it, and Rav PineHas bar Ami challenged them.
answer.outcome: They came before Rava, who called them white geese who strip people of their cloaks and ruled it did not count because the boat was seized after the debtor died.
answer.summary: Yeimar bar Hashu sent his agent to seize a boat the dead debtor left behind. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna rebuked him for harming other creditors, then seized the boat themselves, one steering with an oar and the other pulling with a rope, each claiming all of it. When challenged, they took the case to Rava, who scolded them as white geese who take people's cloaks and ruled that seizure must occur while the debtor is alive.

answer.actor: Rav Malkiyyu
answer.event: Rav Malkiyyu married a deaf-mute neighbor to a woman and had him write her a 400-dinar marriage contract from his property.
answer.turn: Rava remarked on how wise Rav Malkiyyu was, giving his reasoning that a man would buy a maidservant for such a person, so a wife who is also a servant is all the better.
answer.outcome: The contract stood and Rava endorsed the move.
answer.summary: A deaf-mute man lived near Rav Malkiyyu. Rav Malkiyyu married him to a woman and had him write her a marriage contract of 400 dinars from his own property. Rava praised him as a wise man, explaining that if the man would be given a maidservant to serve him, a wife who serves and is also a wife is a double benefit.

answer.actor: A man who made an eiruv with onions, and Rabbi Meir
answer.event: While Rabbi Meir spent Shabbat in Ardiska, a man told him he had made an eiruv with onions to walk to Tiv'in.
answer.turn: Rabbi Meir did not accept the onion eiruv.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Meir made him stay within his four cubits.
answer.summary: Rabbi Meir once spent Shabbat in Ardiska. A man came to him and said he had set up an eiruv with onions so he could continue to Tiv'in. Rabbi Meir treated the eiruv as invalid and made the man remain within his four cubits.
answer.missing: Why the eiruv fails is only inferred; the story is cited as a challenge to a legal ruling.

answer.actor: Rabbi Zeira and then Rava, teaching in Mehoza
answer.event: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the crowd stoned him with etrogim.
answer.turn: Rava taught first that a convert may marry a priest's daughter and was carried on silk, then taught that a convert may marry a mamzeret.
answer.outcome: The people said he had forfeited his earlier honor, and Rava replied that he had done them good by widening their options.
answer.summary: In Mehoza, Rabbi Zeira taught that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the converts present pelted him with etrogim. Rava taught the same town that a convert may marry a priest's daughter, and they carried him on silk. When he then taught the mamzeret ruling too, they said he had lost the honor he had won; he answered that he had done them good, as converts could now marry from either group.

answer.missing: Only a description of Rabbi Abbahu's habitual practice of carrying or not carrying a lamp depending on locale, followed by legal analysis of it; no single event.

answer.actor: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya, and his father-in-law Rabbi Yannai
answer.event: Yehuda used to come home every Shabbat eve preceded by a pillar of fire that Rabbi Yannai saw, but one day he stayed absorbed in study.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, assumed Yehuda had died and had his bed overturned.
answer.outcome: The remark came true like an error from a ruler, and Yehuda died.
answer.summary: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya, studied in the study hall and came home each Shabbat eve, with a pillar of fire going before him that Rabbi Yannai could see. One day he got caught up in study and did not come. Rabbi Yannai saw no sign and said to turn his bed over, since Yehuda would never have missed his time if alive. His words proved to be like an error from a ruler, and Yehuda died.

answer.actor: A man selling glass beads and a woman
answer.event: A woman asked a bead seller for a string, and he asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it; she answered 'Give, give.'
answer.turn: Rav Hama ruled that 'give, give' means nothing, since she was mocking him.
answer.outcome: She is not betrothed.
answer.summary: A man was selling glass beads when a woman asked for a string. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she said only 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that such a phrase is nothing, as she was mocking him and did not agree, so there was no betrothal.

answer.actor: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov
answer.event: Rav Aha found his son Rav Ya'akov, whom he had sent to Abaye, was not sharp, and went to study himself, and Abaye arranged that he be forced to sleep in the haunted study hall.
answer.turn: A seven-headed demon appeared to Rav Aha, and with each bow he made a head fell off.
answer.outcome: The demon died and Rav Aha told the townspeople next morning that had a miracle not occurred, they would have endangered him.
answer.summary: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov sent his son to study with Abaye, but found the son's learning dull, so he said he would go and study himself. Abaye, hearing he was coming, knew a demon haunted the study hall, and told the townspeople not to give Rav Aha lodging, hoping for a miracle. Rav Aha spent the night there, the demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent, and with each bow of his prayer a head fell off until it died. In the morning he told the townspeople they had put him in danger.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yosei and Elijah
answer.event: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah and asked how a wife is a man's helper.
answer.turn: Elijah answered that she turns raw wheat and flax into bread and clothing.
answer.outcome: The encounter ends with Elijah's answer.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah the prophet and asked in what way a woman is a helper to a man. Elijah answered that a man brings wheat and flax, which he cannot eat or wear raw, and his wife prepares them, so she lights up his eyes and stands him on his feet.
answer.missing: It is a brief encounter built around a question and answer, with no real turn or consequence.

answer.actor: Rav Sheshet and the Rabbis
answer.event: The Rabbis urged Rav Sheshet to marry and have sons, and he replied that his daughter's sons are his sons.
answer.turn: The Gemara explains he was only putting them off because he had become impotent from Rav Huna's discourses.
answer.outcome: The reply is read as an evasion, not as a legal position.
answer.summary: The Rabbis told Rav Sheshet to marry a woman and have sons, and he answered that his daughter's sons count as his sons. The Gemara explains he was only brushing them off, as he had become impotent from sitting through Rav Huna's long discourses.
answer.missing: Mostly a legal argument; the exchange is only a brief anecdote used as a proof.

answer.actor: Me'oret and her slave
answer.event: Me'oret made her slave perform three of the dangerous acts and he died.
answer.turn: This was raised as an objection to Abaye's ruling that out-of-order acts only weaken.
answer.outcome: The Gemara explains that the slave was already weak.
answer.summary: Me'oret once made her slave do three of the listed dangerous acts, and he died. This was raised as a challenge to Abaye, who said that doing them out of order only weakens a person. The answer was that the slave was weak to begin with.
answer.missing: The incident is told in a single clause as a legal objection, with no detail of the event.
Only rulings by Rav Asi and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in reply to people being taunted as sons of Arameans; no event is told.

answer.actor: Ameimar
answer.event: Ameimar permitted Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza, and Rav Ashi challenged him.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi pointed out that several schools did not teach the lenient ruling.
answer.outcome: Ameimar did not accept the challenge, as he relied on what he heard directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.
answer.summary: Ameimar allowed Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza. Rav Ashi asked what his basis was, noting that the schools of Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid did not teach the lenient ruling. Ameimar still did not accept it from him, because he had heard it directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages
answer.event: In Rabbi's days the Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites into the congregation.
answer.turn: Rabbi said that even if they permitted their own share, no one could permit the altar's share.
answer.outcome: The proposal was blocked.
answer.summary: In the days of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi the Sages wanted to permit the Gibeonites to marry into the community. Rabbi answered that they could waive their own share, but nobody could waive the altar's share. The proposal did not go forward.
answer.missing: The text implies but does not state that the proposal failed.

answer.actor: A Roman man and a woman
answer.event: A Roman asked a woman to marry him, she refused, and he ate pomegranates in front of her without giving her any.
answer.turn: She swallowed her saliva and fell ill, and he then offered to cure her if she would marry him and she agreed.
answer.outcome: He had her spit out her saliva while he ate, until something like a green leaf came out and she was cured.
answer.summary: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she said no. He peeled pomegranates and ate them in front of her, and her mouth watered so much that she swallowed it all and became ill. He then offered to cure her if she would marry him, she agreed, and he ate again while telling her to spit out her saliva. She did so until something like a green leaf came out and she was healed.

answer.actor: Rav Hamnuna and Ulla
answer.event: Ulla praised Rav Hamnuna as a great man, but wished Harpanya were not his city.
answer.turn: Rav Hamnuna was ashamed; Ulla asked where he paid his poll tax, and learned it was Pum Nahara.
answer.outcome: Ulla concluded Rav Hamnuna was from Pum Nahara, not Harpanya, so his lineage was fine.
answer.summary: Rav Hamnuna sat before Ulla studying, and Ulla exclaimed what a man he was, if only Harpanya were not his city. Rav Hamnuna was ashamed. Ulla asked where he paid his poll tax, and when he said Pum Nahara, Ulla said that makes him from Pum Nahara, so his lineage is unflawed.

answer.actor: A man who deposited a goblet, and Rav Nahman
answer.event: A man left a silver goblet in Hasa's house, and Hasa died without saying anything about it.
answer.turn: The claimants came before Rav Nahman, who noted Hasa was not wealthy and the depositor gave a distinguishing mark.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the depositor, with the caveat that it holds only if he does not regularly come and go there.
answer.summary: A man deposited a silver goblet in the house of Hasa, who then died without leaving instructions. They came to Rav Nahman, who said he knew Hasa was not wealthy and that the depositor had given an identifying mark. He ruled for the depositor, adding that this holds only if the claimant is not someone who regularly came and went there.
answer.missing: The ruling in favor of the depositor is implied rather than stated outright.

answer.actor: A husband, his first wife, and Rava
answer.event: A woman brought her husband two maidservants as dowry, he married a second wife and gave one maidservant to her.
answer.turn: The first wife came before Rava and cried out.
answer.outcome: Rava ignored her, since the house gained from the maidservant's work.
answer.summary: A woman brought her husband two maidservants. He married another wife and gave one of the maidservants to her. The first wife came before Rava and cried out, but Rava paid no attention. Observers assumed he held that what the husband did was valid, but the real reason was that the household gained from it.

answer.actor: Ravina and Rav Ashi
answer.event: Ravina examined a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia while his teacher Rav Ashi was alive, and Rav Ashi asked why he did so.
answer.turn: Ravina cited Rav Hamnuna, Rav Ashi said that tradition says he did not rule, and Ravina answered that Rav Hamnuna ruled in the time of his colleague-teacher Rav Hisda.
answer.outcome: Ravina argued that he too is Rav Ashi's disciple-colleague and so could rule.
answer.summary: Ravina examined a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia while his teacher Rav Ashi was alive, and Rav Ashi asked why he had done that. Ravina cited Rav Hamnuna, who ruled while Rav Hisda lived. Rav Ashi said the tradition is that he did not rule, and Ravina replied that both traditions are true, since Rav Hamnuna held back only during his main teacher's life, and he himself is a disciple-colleague of Rav Ashi.
answer.missing: Rav Ashi's reaction to the final argument is not given.

answer.actor: A man who sold his mother's marriage contract, and Rava
answer.event: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract on condition he would not reimburse if she objected.
answer.turn: His mother died without objecting, and he came and objected himself.
answer.outcome: Rava rejected the claim that he stands in his mother's place, since he had guaranteed against his own objections.
answer.summary: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract for a payment, and said he would not reimburse the buyer if his mother objected. She died without objecting, but he came and contested the sale himself. Rami bar Hama thought he could stand in his mother's place, but Rava answered that though he had not guaranteed against her objection, he had guaranteed against his own.

answer.actor: Rabbi Zeira
answer.event: Rabbi Zeira avoided his teacher Rav Yehuda because he wanted to go up to Eretz Yisrael.
answer.turn: Rav Yehuda held that going up from Babylonia violates a positive commandment.
answer.outcome: No outcome is given in the passage; the discussion moves to the verse debate.
answer.summary: Rabbi Zeira wanted to go up to Eretz Yisrael, but his teacher Rav Yehuda held that doing so violated a positive commandment, so Rabbi Zeira kept out of his sight. The passage then turns to the scriptural debate between them.
answer.missing: What happened to Rabbi Zeira, or whether he went, is not told; the passage cuts off into a verse citation.

answer.actor: Rav Hamnuna, sent by Rav Hisda
answer.event: Rav Hamnuna goes to ostracize the Elders of Nezonya for skipping Rav Hisda's lecture, but they say Rav Hisda never answered their question and then pose one Hamnuna cannot answer.
answer.turn: Hamnuna cannot answer their question about a castrated slave and they mock his name, calling him Karnuna.
answer.outcome: He returns to Rav Hisda, who tells him the question could have been answered from a mishna and baraita.
answer.summary: The Elders of Nezonya stayed away from Rav Hisda's lecture, so he sent Rav Hamnuna to ostracize them. They told him they had once asked Hisda a question he never resolved, so Hamnuna invited them to ask him. He could not answer their question about a castrated slave, and they mocked him by calling him Karnuna, a cold fish, instead of Hamnuna. He went back to Rav Hisda, who said the answer was in a known baraita.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: Sages returning from Pelandarsin find their boat has sailed out to sea on Shabbat; two walk the whole boat, two stay within four cubits.
answer.turn: The sages split in how they behave on the boat.
answer.outcome: Gamliel and Elazar ben Azarya walked about, while Yehoshua and Akiva stringently stayed put.
answer.summary: A group of sages, including Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva, were traveling by boat when it set sail on Shabbat. Gamliel and Elazar ben Azarya walked the whole boat, while Yehoshua and Akiva did not move beyond four cubits, being stringent with themselves. The passage cites this only as a proof for a legal point.
answer.missing: The incident is only cited as evidence in a legal argument, with no real turn or ending.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel
answer.event: Funerals had become so costly that relatives abandoned the dead; Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in plain linen.
answer.turn: Gamliel's self-deprecating example broke the custom of opulent burials.
answer.outcome: All the people followed him, and today even rough cloth worth a zuz is customary.
answer.summary: Burial had become so expensive that relatives sometimes left the dead and fled. Rabban Gamliel then instructed that he be buried in plain linen garments. All the people followed his example, and Rav Pappa notes that even a one-zuz rough cloth is now accepted.

answer.actor: Rav Anan
answer.event: Rav Anan, whom Elijah regularly taught, unwittingly caused a perversion of justice and Elijah left.
answer.turn: Elijah left, returned frightening after Anan fasted, and Anan hid in a box to continue learning.
answer.outcome: Anan sat in a box before Elijah until he learned the whole Seder, giving rise to Seder Eliyahu Rabba and Zuta.
answer.summary: A man brought Rav Anan a gift and was sent to Rav Nahman, who favored him as a supposed relative, leaving a litigant at a loss and justice perverted. Elijah, who used to teach Rav Anan, left. Anan fasted and prayed and Elijah returned, but now he scared him. Anan hid in a box and sat before him until Elijah taught him the entire Seder.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Tzadok
answer.event: Each rabbi is propositioned by a noblewoman and escapes sin by extraordinary means.
answer.turn: Hanina covers himself with boils and later hides in a dangerous bathhouse; Tzadok sits in a hot oven to show the fate of sinners.
answer.outcome: Hanina is protected overnight by angelic soldiers; the noblewoman gives up on Tzadok, saying she would not have troubled him had she known.
answer.summary: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. He recited a formula that covered him with boils, she healed him by magic, and he fled to a demon-infested bathhouse where angels guarded him all night. Rabbi Tzadok was similarly propositioned, asked for food, and when she heated non-kosher food he climbed into the oven. He said one who does this falls into the fire of Gehenna, and she relented.

answer.actor: The people of Neharde'a and Rav Nahman
answer.event: During a drought everyone in Neharde'a sold their mansions to buy wheat.
answer.turn: Wheat arrived, so the sales were unnecessary.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled the mansions must be returned to their former owners.
answer.summary: During a drought in Neharde'a, everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat. Then wheat arrived, making the sales unnecessary. Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions be returned to their original owners.
answer.missing: It is cited as a legal proof, with the story told very briefly.

answer.actor: Rav Dimi and Abaye
answer.event: Abaye challenges Rav Dimi over Rabbi Yohanan's statement; Dimi falls silent, Abaye offers the answer himself, and Dimi praises him.
answer.turn: Dimi is left without an answer until Abaye supplies it.
answer.outcome: Dimi tells Abaye he must have been present in the study hall when Rabbi Yohanan taught it.
answer.summary: Abaye challenged Rav Dimi with a contradiction in Rabbi Yohanan's rulings. Dimi was silent, unable to answer, so Abaye suggested a distinction based on the verse about Egyptian converts. Dimi replied that Abaye must have been present in the study hall when Yohanan taught it.
answer.missing: This is a brief scholarly exchange rather than a full story with an event and a lasting turn.

answer.actor: Rav Adda bar Ahava, his host, and Rav Beivai
answer.event: Rav Adda's host (a convert's son) and Rav Beivai quarrel over who should hold authority in the city and bring it to Rav Yosef.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef says converts cannot hold appointments, but Adda asks about a Jewish mother and Yosef finds the host eligible.
answer.outcome: Rav Beivai oversees religious matters and the host the city's affairs; Abaye draws the moral to host someone who can plead one's case.
answer.summary: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host and Rav Beivai quarreled over who would manage the city's affairs and came before Rav Yosef. Yosef first said appointments must come from among one's brothers, which excluded converts. Adda asked about someone whose mother is Jewish, and Yosef said he qualified. So Rav Beivai took charge of religious matters and the host of the city's affairs, and Abaye said to host someone like Adda who can plead for you.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar
answer.event: Rabbi Elazar doubts that Shmuel taught a ruling and goes to his lodging to ask him directly.
answer.turn: Shmuel confirms the ruling, but Elazar objects from Shmuel's own earlier statement.
answer.outcome: Shmuel is silent and gives no answer.
answer.summary: Rav Beruna taught a ruling in Shmuel's name, and Rabbi Elazar doubted it. He had Beruna show him Shmuel's lodging and asked Shmuel himself, who confirmed it. Elazar then pointed out that Shmuel had once said that eiruv law follows only the mishna's wording, which implied the opposite. Shmuel was silent.

answer.actor: The heirs of a man who willed a palm tree to his daughter
answer.event: A man bequeathed a palm tree to his daughter but died owning only two half-shares of palm trees, which the heirs wanted to give her.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi asks whether people call two half-trees a palm tree.
answer.outcome: Rav Mordekhai reports in Rava's name that people do, so the heirs may give her the two halves.
answer.summary: A man told his heirs he was leaving a palm tree to his daughter, but died owning only two half-shares of palm trees. Rav Ashi wondered if that counts as a palm tree. Rav Mordekhai reported in Rava's name that people do call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs may give her those.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon
answer.event: Rabbi Tarfon would bend down so his mother could climb into and out of bed, and boasted of it in the study hall.
answer.turn: The sages told him he had not reached even half of the honor due, asking if he would stay unembarrassed if she threw his purse in the sea.
answer.outcome: He is rebuked, showing that true honor goes further.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tarfon would bend over so his mother could step on him to get in and out of bed. He praised himself in the study hall for this. The sages told him he had not reached half of the honor due her, since he had not yet endured her throwing his purse into the sea without shaming her.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok
answer.event: At the wedding of Rabban Gamliel's son, Gamliel stood and served drinks to the sages, and Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup.
answer.turn: Eliezer objects that the Nasi should not serve them, and Yehoshua and Tzadok argue that even Abraham and God serve.
answer.outcome: They show that even a Nasi may forgo his honor, so the others may accept.
answer.summary: At the wedding of Rabban Gamliel's son, Gamliel stood and served drinks to Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok. Eliezer refused the cup but Yehoshua accepted it, and Eliezer protested. Yehoshua said Abraham, the greatest of his generation, served his guests. Tzadok added that God Himself serves everyone, so Gamliel could serve them too.

answer.actor: Rav Gamda and the sages Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi
answer.event: When Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled against her husband, three sages ruled on her worn clothes and Rav Gamda rebuked them.
answer.turn: Rav Gamda accuses them of ruling to favor or against the great Rav Zevid when Rava never resolved the question.
answer.outcome: The matter is left unresolved: if she seized the clothes they are not taken, and if not they are not given.
answer.summary: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled against her husband while holding a garment. Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi ruled on whether she lost her worn clothes, with Rav Gamda sitting with them. Rav Gamda objected that they were bending the law because Rav Zevid was a great man, since Rava never resolved the question. The conclusion was that whatever she seized stays, and what she did not seize is not given.
answer.missing: The two versions of the ruling are told in parallel.

answer.actor: Peleimu
answer.event: Peleimu, who mocked Satan daily, was visited on the eve of Yom Kippur by Satan disguised as a pauper.
answer.turn: The pauper behaved repulsively and, after being berated, feigned death so Peleimu was accused of murder.
answer.outcome: Satan revealed himself and told Peleimu to say, 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan' rather than mock him.
answer.summary: Peleimu used to say daily, An arrow in Satan's eye. On Yom Kippur eve Satan came as a pauper and got himself seated at the table, where he acted revoltingly and spat in a cup. When Peleimu's household berated him, he pretended to die, people cried that Peleimu had killed a man, and Peleimu fled. Satan then revealed himself and told Peleimu to say instead, May the Merciful One rebuke Satan.

answer.actor: The son of a widow
answer.event: He asks Rabbi Eliezer whose request for water to honor first when both parents ask, and is told to put his father first.
answer.turn: He then asks Rabbi Yehoshua what if his mother is divorced.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua says his tear-filled eyelashes show he is a widow's son and sarcastically tells him to give them each water and call them like chickens.
answer.summary: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer which parent to serve first if both ask for water, and was told to honor his father. He asked Rabbi Yehoshua the same and got the same answer. When he asked what if his mother were divorced, Yehoshua said it was clear from his eyelashes that he was a widow's son and sarcastically told him to pour them water and squawk at them like chickens.

answer.actor: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
answer.event: Rabbi Abbahu reports in Rabbi Yohanan's name a halakha, and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turn their faces away.
answer.turn: Their turning away signals disagreement without contradicting him out of respect.
answer.outcome: From this it is concluded that Rabbi Yohanan did not hold that way.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abbahu sat and said in Rabbi Yohanan's name that the law follows Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turned their faces away, silently disagreeing. Another version says Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba said it. The Gemara uses this to infer what Rabbi Yohanan held.
answer.missing: A brief incident used as legal evidence, without a clear ending of its own.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman conditionally, and the Sages
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman conditionally and then had intercourse with her.
answer.turn: The condition was not clearly fulfilled, so the Sages could not declare the betrothal void.
answer.outcome: The Sages forced him to give her a bill of divorce.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman on condition and then had relations with her. The Sages did not have the authority to free her without a bill of divorce, so they made him give her one.
answer.missing: The incident is told in one line with no named people.

answer.actor: A maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household and Rabbi
answer.event: The maidservant immersed, came up, and a bone was found between her teeth.
answer.turn: The bone meant the immersion may not have covered her whole body.
answer.outcome: Rabbi required her to immerse again.
answer.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi's household immersed herself. When she came up, a bone was found between her teeth. Rabbi made her immerse a second time.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and his student Abaye
answer.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a halakha, and Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it, citing Rami bar Abba and Rav Huna and the three lessons Rav Yosef drew from it.
answer.turn: Abaye showed the teacher had forgotten his own teaching (the text explains he had been ill and forgot his learning).
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef's response is not shown; the halakha is later ruled to follow it.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain halakha from his teachers. His student Abaye told him that he had taught it to them himself, and quoted the statement and the three lessons Rav Yosef drew from it. The text explains that Rav Yosef had been ill and had forgotten his learning.
answer.missing: Rav Yosef's reaction to being reminded, and a clear ending.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa
answer.event: Rav Pappa served drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding and poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Yehuda.
answer.turn: Rav Yitzhak did not stand up for him.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
answer.summary: At his son Abba Mar's wedding, Rav Pappa went around serving drinks. When he poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Yehuda, Rav Yitzhak did not stand up before him. Rav Pappa was angry.

answer.actor: A man whose betrothed wife had died, and the sages Rav Nahman, Ulla, Avimei and Rav Hiyya bar Ami
answer.event: A man whose betrothed had died came before sitting sages, who told him to bury her or pay her marriage contract.
answer.turn: Rav Hiyya objected, citing a teaching that a husband does not inherit from a betrothed wife.
answer.outcome: No outcome for the man is shown; the objection leads into a legal discussion.
answer.summary: Several sages were sitting together when a man came whose betrothed had died. They told him to bury her or pay her marriage contract. Rav Hiyya objected in surprise and quoted a teaching that a husband does not inherit his betrothed wife.
answer.missing: What the man actually did or how the case ended.

answer.actor: Rav Yehezkel and his sons Rami and Rav Yehuda
answer.event: Rav Yehezkel taught Rami a mishna, and his son Rav Yehuda objected that he should teach it differently, and they argued over the wording.
answer.turn: Rav Yehezkel countered that Yehuda's version had the same problem in the second half, and Yehuda answered it.
answer.outcome: Later Shmuel told Rav Yehuda not to speak to his father so bluntly, and taught how to correct a father respectfully.
answer.summary: Rav Yehezkel taught his son Rami a mishna. His other son, Rav Yehuda, told him not to teach it that way and proposed a reversed wording. Their father answered that the same objection applied to the other half, and Yehuda explained the difference. Shmuel later told Yehuda he was speaking disrespectfully to his father and should correct him gently by quoting the verse.

answer.actor: Rav Huna and Rav Hamnuna
answer.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna, who asked to meet him, and saw he wore no head cloth.
answer.turn: Rav Hamnuna said he was unmarried.
answer.outcome: Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to come before him again until he married.
answer.summary: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man, and Rav Huna asked to see him. When Rav Hamnuna came, Rav Huna saw he wore no head cloth and asked why. Hamnuna said he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and said he should not see his face until he married.

answer.actor: Pishon the camel driver and his wife
answer.event: Beit Hillel cited the case of Pishon the camel driver, whose wife refused him in his absence.
answer.turn: Beit Shammai said Pishon had mismanaged her property, so the Sages penalized him.
answer.outcome: The Sages treated it as a special case and allowed the refusal.
answer.summary: Beit Hillel pointed to Pishon the camel driver, whose wife annulled the marriage without his being present. Beit Shammai said he had not looked after her property properly, so the Sages dealt with him by a defective standard. The text only alludes to the incident as a precedent.
answer.missing: The actual events of Pishon's case; it is only referred to inside a dispute.

answer.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
answer.event: They bought a maidservant to be paid in copper coins, and gave a piece of silver as collateral because they had no money.
answer.turn: The maidservant's price rose, and the sellers wanted to cancel the sale.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled there were no coins and no silver given, so there was no valid sale.
answer.summary: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin bought a maidservant, to be paid for in copper coins. They had no coins, so they left a piece of silver as collateral. Her price then went up, and they came before Rabbi Ami. He ruled that no coins had been paid and the collateral did not count, so there was no sale.

answer.actor: Mar Shmuel
answer.event: A lentil bread in Mar Shmuel's days was thrown to his dog.
answer.turn: The dog would not eat it.
answer.outcome: This is used as an objection to Rav's ruling; it is answered in the next segment (the bread was mixed grain).
answer.summary: In Mar Shmuel's days there was a lentil bread that he threw to his dog, and even the dog would not eat it. It is cited as a challenge to a ruling that lentil bread may be used for an eiruv.
answer.missing: Who baked it and why; the story is only an objection to a ruling.

answer.actor: A Galilean woman
answer.event: She tried to invite her friend to come and be fed milk.
answer.turn: Her imprecise pronunciation turned the words into a different phrase.
answer.outcome: She actually told her friend 'may a lioness eat you'.
answer.summary: A Galilean woman wanted to say to her friend, 'Come and I will feed you milk.' Because Galileans did not pronounce the guttural letters properly, what came out was 'My neighbor, may a lioness eat you.'

answer.actor: Bar Shatya and the witnesses, with Rav Ashi
answer.event: Bar Shatya, who was sometimes insane, sold property, and two witnesses said he was healthy when he sold it while two others said he was insane.
answer.turn: The two conflicting testimonies cancelled each other out.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi ruled the land stays in Bar Shatya's possession.
answer.summary: Bar Shatya, a man who sometimes went insane, sold land. Two witnesses came to say he was healthy at the time, and two others said he was insane. Rav Ashi ruled to set the two pairs against each other and leave the land with Bar Shatya.

answer.actor: Rav Hisda, Rava, and Elijah or Yosef the demon
answer.event: Seven teachings said on Shabbat morning before Rav Hisda in Sura were repeated before Rava in Pumbedita by the end of that Shabbat.
answer.turn: Someone must have carried them, though the distance was too far to walk on Shabbat.
answer.outcome: The Gemara suggests Elijah, then rejects the proof, saying it may have been Yosef the demon.
answer.summary: Seven teachings were said on Shabbat morning before Rav Hisda in Sura and again toward the end of the same Shabbat before Rava in Pumbedita. The distance was too great to walk. Elijah might have carried them by leaping through the air, but it may equally have been Yosef the demon, who does not keep Shabbat.
answer.missing: Who really carried them; the passage is cited as a proof and left open.

answer.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of Bar Elyashiv
answer.event: She claimed her marriage contract from the orphans and was bringing them to court.
answer.turn: The orphans told her it was demeaning that she go in house clothes, so she dressed in all her clothes.
answer.outcome: Before Ravina, he ruled that the court appraises the clothes on a widow, so what she wore counted against her payment.
answer.summary: A woman of the Bar Elyashiv family was claiming her marriage contract from the orphans and taking them to court. They told her it was demeaning to them that she appear in plain house clothes, so she put on all her clothes. When they came before Ravina, he ruled that the court appraises the clothes on a widow and counts them toward her payment.

answer.actor: Rava
answer.event: Rava served drinks at his son's wedding and poured cups for sages.
answer.turn: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna stood before him, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas did not.
answer.outcome: Rava became angry and asked whether those who stood were sages and the others were not.
answer.summary: At his son's wedding Rava served drinks. When he poured for Rav Pappa and Rav Huna they stood up before him, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas did not. Rava got angry and asked whether some of them were sages and some were not.

answer.actor: King Yannai, Elazar ben Po'ira, Yehuda ben Gedidya and the Pharisee sages
answer.event: After conquering sixty cities, Yannai held a feast for the sages, where Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees resented him.
answer.turn: Yannai had them stand before his frontplate, Yehuda ben Gedidya told him to give up the priesthood, and the sages were expelled in anger.
answer.outcome: Elazar urged killing them, and the sages were killed and the world was desolate of Torah until Shimon ben Shatah restored it.
answer.summary: King Yannai returned from conquering sixty cities and held a feast for the sages. Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees resented him and suggested testing them with the frontplate. Yehuda ben Gedidya told Yannai to give up the priesthood, since a rumor said his mother had been a captive, and the sages were driven out in rage. Elazar then urged Yannai to crush them, and all the sages were killed until Shimon ben Shatah restored the Torah.

answer.actor: Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zerika
answer.event: A question was put to Rabbi Ami about a slave who gave himself to an army and whether the master may take his value.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yirmeya sent Rabbi Zerika to look and he found a baraita about a house seized by force; this was challenged as not comparable.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami sent a message ruling that the master may take the value.
answer.summary: Rabbi Ami was asked about a slave who gave himself over to an army and whom the master could not recover. Rabbi Yirmeya sent Rabbi Zerika to check his teachings, and he found a baraita permitting a man to take the value of a house seized by force. That was challenged, but Rabbi Ami finally sent word that the master may take the slave's value.
answer.missing: It is mostly a legal inquiry with a few steps of action.

answer.actor: Rav
answer.event: Rav walked in among the sheaves in a field and saw them waving in the wind.
answer.turn: He spoke to them as if they were boasting.
answer.outcome: He told them that doing business is better than farming them; Rava then adds a related saying.
answer.summary: Rav went into a field among the sheaves and saw them swaying in the wind. He said to them that they could wave if they liked, but business is better than farming them. Rava then gave a related saying about the poor returns of land.
answer.missing: No real turn or ending; it is a brief anecdote used to make a point.

answer.actor: Rabbi Eliezer
answer.event: Missing the study hall, Rabbi Eliezer met Rabbi Asi and asked what had been taught there.
answer.turn: Told the law follows Rabbi Yosei, he inferred that only a single authority disagrees.
answer.outcome: The exchange moves into legal argument; Rabbi Asi's answer comes in the following segment.
answer.summary: Rabbi Eliezer did not attend the study hall, so he met Rabbi Asi, who was standing, and asked what had been said. Rabbi Asi reported that Rabbi Yohanan ruled like Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Eliezer asked whether this implies a lone dissenter, and Rabbi Asi answered yes, citing a baraita.
answer.missing: There is little event beyond a chance meeting and a legal exchange; no real turn or resolution.

answer.actor: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov
answer.event: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov was struck by suskhinta, the illness caused by holding back from urinating during Rav Huna's long lectures, and was hung from the cedar pillar of the study hall.
answer.turn: A green substance came out of him and he was cured.
answer.outcome: He said that of sixty elders who all became impotent from Rav Huna's discourse, he alone escaped, by wisdom preserving its owner.
answer.summary: Several sages, including Rav Giddel, Rav Helbo and Rav Sheshet, became impotent from holding back during Rav Huna's lectures. Rav Aha bar Ya'akov fell ill with the same condition, was hung from the cedar pillar of the study hall, and a green substance emerged, healing him. He later said that of sixty elders only he escaped, since wisdom preserves its possessor.

answer.actor: Dama ben Netina
answer.event: Sitting among Rome's nobles in a gold cloak, Dama was approached by his mother, who tore the cloak off, hit him on the head and spat in his face.
answer.turn: He was publicly humiliated by his own mother.
answer.outcome: He did not shame her in return.
answer.summary: Dama ben Netina once sat among the nobles of Rome wearing a fine gold cloak. His mother came, tore the garment from him, smacked his head and spat in his face. He did not embarrass her.

answer.actor: The household of the prince and the judges Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha and Rabbi Abba
answer.event: The prince's household seized an orphans' maidservant for a debt, and the judges approved the seizure.
answer.turn: Rabbi Abba accused the judges of currying favor and noted that Reish Lakish had earlier reversed a judgment made under Rabbi Tarfon's rule.
answer.outcome: Not stated within the passage; only an objection is left standing.
answer.summary: The prince's household seized an orphans' maidservant in an alley to collect a debt. Judges including Rabbi Abbahu approved it as well done. Rabbi Abba objected that they were flattering the household, since Reish Lakish had overturned a similar ruling.
answer.missing: What the judges did after Rabbi Abba's objection; the case's final result.

answer.actor: A fox and the people who weighed the turnip
answer.event: A fox nested in a turnip, and the turnip was weighed.
answer.turn: Even without the hollowed space it weighed sixty litra.
answer.outcome: Offered as proof that giant future wheat is not implausible.
answer.summary: A fox once made its nest inside a turnip. People weighed the turnip and found, even discounting the dug-out space, that it weighed sixty litra by the Tzippori measure. This is cited to show that wheat as large as ox kidneys is not far-fetched.
answer.missing: The fox incident is a one-line proof within a homiletic prediction; no actors, setting or resolution are given.

answer.actor: Rava and Rav Safra
answer.event: Rav Safra challenged Rava that the Tigris separates Akistefon and Ardeshir by more than 141 and a third cubits, yet they are treated as one city.
answer.turn: Rava went out and showed him the foundations of a wall submerged in the Tigris about seventy cubits away.
answer.outcome: The challenge was answered, because the cities are linked by the submerged wall.
answer.summary: Rav Safra pointed out to Rava that the Tigris separates Akistefon and Ardeshir by more than the allowed distance, yet they are measured as a single city. Rava went out and showed him the foundations of a wall submerged in the river at seventy cubits and a remainder. That linked the two cities and answered the objection.

answer.actor: Rav Nahman
answer.event: A woman from Mehoza married to a man of Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman, who noticed from her voice that she was from Mehoza.
answer.turn: He first ruled by the Babylonian custom, but when told she married into Neharde'a he reversed to the Neharde'a custom.
answer.outcome: He ruled that Neharde'a and its towns follow Shmuel, extending as far as the Neharde'a kav measure is used.
answer.summary: A woman of Mehoza who had married into Neharde'a came with her husband before Rav Nahman. Hearing her accent, he said Babylonia follows Rav. When told she was married to a Neharde'a man, he said that Neharde'a and its towns follow Shmuel, and defined Neharde'a's boundary by its measures.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, Rabbi Yishmael, Rav Shemen bar Abba
answer.event: Rav Dimi and Ravin reported that a case about a wife's sustenance came before Rabbi in Beit She'arim and Rabbi Yishmael in Tzippori, with opposite rulings.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan questioned why one sage refused sustenance, and Rav Shemen bar Abba said Shmuel had already explained it as a case where the husband was heard to be dead.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan responded in astonishment, 'Have you gone that far?'
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported that one case of a wife's sustenance came before Rabbi and another before Rabbi Yishmael, and they ruled in opposite ways. Rabbi Yohanan was puzzled by the one who refused it, and Rav Shemen bar Abba said Shmuel in Babylonia had explained it as a case where the husband was reported dead. Rabbi Yohanan answered in astonishment. Ravin's version swaps which judge ruled which way.
answer.missing: The cases' facts and final outcomes are not given; the passage is mostly a legal discussion framed by reports.

answer.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
answer.event: She came before Rav Yosef asking him to set her sustenance, then wine, then silk garments.
answer.turn: When he asked why she needed silk, she replied it was for him, his friends and his friends' friends.
answer.outcome: Her quip ends the account; whether silk was granted is not stated.
answer.summary: A widow, the wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya, came before Rav Yosef and asked for sustenance and wine, which he granted. She then asked for silk, and when he asked why, she said it was for him, his friends and his friends' friends, so she would not be ashamed in front of them.
answer.missing: Whether Rav Yosef granted the silk.

answer.actor: Rabba bar bar Hanna and Abaye
answer.event: Rabba bar bar Hanna said he saw an Arab cut open his camel, which died before it could stop braying.
answer.turn: Abaye answered that the camel was emaciated and so died instantly.
answer.outcome: Abaye's answer neutralized the objection to the earlier ruling.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Hanna said he personally saw an Arab slash open his camel with a sword, and it died before its braying stopped. Abaye said that camel was emaciated and weak, so a normal one would not die so quickly.
answer.missing: The anecdote is a brief eyewitness proof inside a legal argument; no real story arc.

answer.actor: Rav Anan bar Tahalifa and Rav Ashi
answer.event: Each stood as waiter before a master (Mar Shmuel, Rav Kahana) when a strongly aromatic dish was brought.
answer.turn: Without a share they said they would have been endangered by the craving.
answer.outcome: The Gemara draws a general rule that anything fragrant or sharp-tasting should be offered to the waiter.
answer.summary: Rav Anan bar Tahalifa recalled standing before Mar Shmuel as a mushroom dish was served and said he would have been endangered had he not been given some. Rav Ashi told a similar story about turnip slices in vinegar before Rav Kahana. The Gemara concludes that anything aromatic or sharp must be shared with the waiter.
answer.missing: These are brief first-person testimonies for a rule; no developed plot.

answer.actor: Rabbi Pinehas
answer.event: When people sought to make Babylonian lineage the muddled one, Rabbi Pinehas told his servants to carry him off on a stretcher after he spoke two statements in the study hall.
answer.turn: After a decoy ruling he said the lineage statement that Eretz Yisrael is muddled relative to Babylonia, and his servants fled with him.
answer.outcome: Those pursuing could not catch him; they investigated families until they reached powerful ones, found it dangerous and withdrew.
answer.summary: When some sought to cast Babylonian lineage as inferior, Rabbi Pinehas arranged for his servants to carry him away on a stretcher once he had spoken. In the study hall he first stated a decoy ruling, then declared that Eretz Yisrael is muddled relative to Babylonia, and was whisked away. The scholars chased him in vain, then examined families until they reached powerful ones and backed off.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: On his deathbed Rabbi named Babylonian places and the sins or flawed lineage of their inhabitants, including a town whose people trapped fish on Shabbat and apostatized after Rabbi Ahai excommunicated them.
answer.turn: He moved from condemnation to naming Adda bar Ahava of Akra DeAgma.
answer.outcome: The statement is cut off; the following segment finishes it (Adda bar Ahava is in Abraham's lap, Rav Yehuda was born).
answer.summary: As Rabbi lay dying, he said which Babylonian towns were tainted, such as Homanya's Ammonites and Masgariya's mamzerim. He told of Bireta DeSatya, where people trapped fish on Shabbat and apostatized after being excommunicated. He then mentioned Adda bar Ahava of Akra DeAgma, who that day sits in Abraham's lap, and said Rav Yehuda was born.
answer.missing: The end of the deathbed statement is in segment [5]; much of it is a list of places rather than a plotted event.

answer.actor: Rav Ashi
answer.event: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi to testify, but Rav Ashi at first did not remember, and Rav Kahana jogged his memory.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi ultimately remembered and testified, then saw Rav Kahana hesitant to accept it.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi told him he was not relying on Rav Kahana's prompting but had made the effort himself to remember.
answer.summary: Rav Ashi knew testimony relevant to Rav Kahana. Rav Kahana asked if he remembered, and Rav Ashi said no, then Rav Kahana described the incident. Eventually Rav Ashi remembered and testified, and seeing Rav Kahana hesitant he said he had not relied on him but had strained himself to recall.

answer.actor: Ten men and a woman
answer.event: Ten men carried a woman out on a bier as if she were dead and had intercourse with her.
answer.turn: This showed that immoral men are not restrained by being many.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef used it to argue that ten men will join in wrongdoing without shame, as ten will steal a beam together.
answer.summary: Once ten men carried a woman out on a bier as though she were dead and abused her. Rav Yosef cited this, with the example of ten people jointly stealing a beam, to show a group of immoral men feel no shame before each other.
answer.missing: Only a one-line incident, with no names or details, used to support a ruling.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: On his deathbed Rabbi named Babylonian places and the sins or lineage problems of their inhabitants, including a town that trapped fish on Shabbat and apostatized.
answer.turn: He ended by saying that today Adda bar Ahava sits in Abraham's lap and that Rav Yehuda was born.
answer.outcome: The statement ends with Rav Yehuda's birth; the later commentary on the chain of righteous people is not part of the story.
answer.summary: As Rabbi lay dying, he listed Babylonian towns with tainted populations, including Bireta DeSatya, whose people trapped fish on Shabbat and apostatized after being excommunicated. He then said Adda bar Ahava, just circumcised, sits in Abraham's lap, and announced that Rav Yehuda was born that day.
answer.missing: Mostly a list of places; the deathbed utterance has a context but little plot.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
answer.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba found Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with a cheap covering on his head, hurrying a child to the synagogue, and asked what the fuss was.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua answered by citing the verse linking teaching one's children to standing at Horeb.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba then refused to eat before teaching a child, and Rabba bar Rav Huna did likewise.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing a child to the synagogue with a cloth thrown over his head. Asked why, Rabbi Yehoshua said that the Torah links teaching one's children to standing at Mount Sinai. From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat until he had taught a child, and Rabba bar Rav Huna would not eat before bringing a child to the study hall.

answer.actor: Rabbi Ḥama bar Bisa
answer.event: After twelve years in the study hall he returned home, but first sat in the local study hall and sent word ahead, so as not to repeat ben Ḥakhinai's sudden arrival.
answer.turn: His unrecognized son Rabbi Oshaya came and questioned him, and Ḥama saw his sharp learning and lamented not having raised such a son.
answer.outcome: He went home, his son followed, and he stood up before him; his wife scolded that a father does not rise for a son, and Rami bar Ḥama applied the verse about a threefold cord to Oshaya.
answer.summary: Rabbi Ḥama bar Bisa spent twelve years studying away. On returning he resolved not to surprise his wife as ben Ḥakhinai had, so he waited in the study hall and sent word ahead. There a young man he did not recognize questioned him sharply, and Ḥama regretted missing his own son's upbringing. At home he rose before the youth, his wife pointed out he was standing for his own son, and the verse of the threefold cord was applied to the family.

answer.actor: Rami bar Yeḥezkel
answer.event: Visiting Benei Berak, he saw goats grazing under fig trees with honey dripping from the figs and milk from the goats, mixing together.
answer.turn: He recognized it as the meaning of the verse 'a land flowing with milk and honey'.
answer.summary: Rami bar Yeḥezkel visited Benei Berak and saw goats grazing under fig trees. Honey oozed from the figs and milk dripped from the goats, and the two mixed together. He remarked that this is what 'flowing with milk and honey' means.
answer.missing: This is a brief anecdote of observation with no real conflict or resolution.

answer.actor: A woman obliged to take an oath, and Rav Beivai bar Abaye
answer.event: A woman required to swear in Rav Beivai's court was asked by her opponent to swear in her own town; she demanded a document of rights first, and Rav Beivai ordered it written.
answer.turn: Rav Pappi rebuked Rav Beivai, playing on his family's unfortunate lineage, for ordering the document written.
answer.outcome: No resolution of the incident is given; only Rav Pappi's rebuke and the legal reasoning behind it follow.
answer.summary: A woman owed an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court. Her opponent wanted her to swear in town, hoping shame would make her confess. She insisted on first receiving a document of rights, and Rav Beivai told the court to write it. Rav Pappi then rebuked him with a pun on his unlucky family.
answer.missing: How the incident actually ended; the explanation of Rav Pappi's objection is in later segments.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed with a myrtle branch; Rav Aḥa bar Huna and Rav Yosef
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in the marketplace, and Rav Aḥa bar Huna sent the question to Rav Yosef.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef answered with a compromise ruling.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled that the man be flogged (per Rav) and the woman require a bill of divorce (per Shmuel).
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in the marketplace. Rav Aḥa bar Huna asked Rav Yosef what to do. Rav Yosef replied that the man should be flogged and that she should still receive a divorce document, just in case the branch was worth a peruta somewhere.
answer.missing: This is a case and a ruling; no further narrative events.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed with a myrtle branch; Rav Aḥa bar Huna and Rav Yosef
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in the marketplace, and Rav Aḥa bar Huna sent the question to Rav Yosef.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef answered with a compromise ruling.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled that the man be flogged (per Rav) and the woman require a bill of divorce (per Shmuel).
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in the marketplace. Rav Aḥa bar Huna asked Rav Yosef what to do. Rav Yosef replied that the man should be flogged and that she should still receive a divorce document, just in case the branch was worth a peruta somewhere.
answer.missing: This is a case and a ruling; no further narrative events.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef and his student Abaye
answer.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain ruling, and Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it, citing the mishna and Rav Yehuda's statement.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef's memory was lost through illness, and his student corrected him.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef said he had not heard a certain ruling. Abaye replied that Rav Yosef himself had taught it to them, and quoted the mishna and Rav Yehuda's explanation. Rav Yosef's response is not given.
answer.missing: Rav Yosef's reaction; the exchange is mostly a legal citation.

answer.actor: Ameimar and Mar Ukva
answer.event: A man did each of them a small favor (removing a feather from Ameimar's head; covering spittle before Mar Ukva) and then revealed he had a case before them.
answer.turn: Each realized the favor created a bond that compromised impartiality.
answer.outcome: Each judge disqualified himself from hearing the man's case.
answer.summary: While Ameimar was judging, a feather landed on his head and a man removed it. When the man said he had a case before him, Ameimar disqualified himself because of the favor. Likewise a man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva, and Mar Ukva disqualified himself from his case too.

answer.actor: Ulla and Rabbi Elazar
answer.event: Ulla, who used to go up to Eretz Yisrael, died outside the land, and Rabbi Elazar was told.
answer.turn: Rabbi Elazar lamented that the verse about dying in an unclean land was fulfilled; told that Ulla's coffin was being brought to Eretz Yisrael, he said it is not the same as being absorbed in its soil while alive.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Elazar maintained that burial there after death does not equal living there.
answer.summary: Ulla often went up to Eretz Yisrael but died abroad. When Rabbi Elazar heard, he mourned that Ulla had died in an unclean land. Told that the coffin was being brought to Eretz Yisrael, he replied that being absorbed by its soil in life is not like being absorbed after death.

answer.actor: A woman obliged to take an oath, and Rav Beivai bar Abaye
answer.event: A woman required to swear in Rav Beivai's court was asked by her opponent to swear in her own town; she demanded a document of rights first, and Rav Beivai ordered it written.
answer.turn: Rav Pappi rebuked Rav Beivai, playing on his family's unfortunate lineage.
answer.outcome: The incident's end is not given; only the rebuke.
answer.summary: A woman owed an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court. Her opponent wanted her to swear in town, hoping shame would make her confess. She insisted on receiving a document of rights first, and Rav Beivai told the court to write it. Rav Pappi then rebuked him with a pun on his unlucky family.
answer.missing: How the incident ended; the legal reasoning for the rebuke is in later segments.

answer.actor: A man in Jerusalem with much movable property
answer.event: Wanting to give away his movable property as a gift, he was advised the only way was through land, so he acquired a small plot and declared it given to someone together with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels.
answer.turn: He died, and the question arose whether the gift took effect.
answer.outcome: The Sages fulfilled his statement and gave the gifts.
answer.summary: A man in Jerusalem, perhaps ill, wanted to give away a large amount of movable property. Told he could only do so by means of land, he bought a tiny plot and declared it, along with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, given to a certain person. He died, and the Sages carried out his declaration.

answer.actor: A woman visiting her husband's grave, and a guard
answer.event: She had intercourse with a man guarding the body of someone executed by the king; when that body was taken, she suggested they exhume her husband so the guard could claim he had done his job.
answer.turn: The body was stolen and the pair used her husband's corpse as a substitute.
answer.outcome: She had her husband removed from his grave; the incident is cited to show sin is possible even in acute mourning.
answer.summary: A woman went to her husband's grave and there had intercourse with a man guarding a body hung by the king. The body was taken, so she proposed digging up her husband's corpse for the guard to present instead. It is told as proof that even mourners can succumb to temptation.
answer.missing: The incident is only briefly summarized in a commentary's terms.

answer.actor: Avimi, son of Rabbi Abbahu
answer.event: Avimi, though ordained and father of five ordained sons, ran to open the door whenever his father called, answering 'yes, yes' before arriving; one day his father asked for water and fell asleep before he returned.
answer.turn: Avimi did not wake or leave his father but stood bent over him until he awoke.
answer.outcome: His devotion was rewarded: he was helped in his learning and succeeded in interpreting the psalm 'A song to Asaph'.
answer.summary: Avimi honored his father Rabbi Abbahu so carefully that even as a distinguished sage he hurried to open the door and called out in advance. Once his father asked for water and dozed off before it arrived, so Avimi stood over him until he woke. As a reward his learning was aided and he could interpret a psalm.

answer.actor: Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: Rabbi Akiva ridiculed transgressors; Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree and he climbed after her.
answer.turn: Halfway up, the evil inclination left him and said it would have destroyed him if not for heaven's proclamation protecting him.
answer.outcome: Akiva was spared only because of his standing in heaven.
answer.summary: Rabbi Akiva used to mock those who sinned. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree, and he grabbed the trunk and began climbing. Halfway up the evil inclination left him and said that only the heavenly warning to be careful with Akiva and his Torah saved him from being ruined.
